Comparison Note —

**Heat pump vs gas furnace operating cost comparison** is the question every homeowner faces when their heating system needs replacement. The short answer: it depends on your local electricity and natural gas prices, your climate, and your equipment efficiency. A heat pump with a COP of 3.0 can deliver 3 units of heat for every unit of electricity consumed, making it potentially cheaper to run than a gas furnace even when electricity costs more per unit than gas. But in extreme cold climates, gas furnaces become more cost-effective below approximately 25°F. This guide provides **real monthly cost data by climate zone, fuel price trends through 2026, COP vs AFUE explanations, break-even analysis, and an interactive calculator** so you can plug in your actual numbers and get a definitive answer for your home.

### Quick Answer

*   Heat pumps cost **$50-$150/month** to operate vs **$80-$200/month** for gas furnaces in cold climates
*   In mild climates (zones 1-3), heat pumps are **30-50% cheaper** to run than gas furnaces
*   In extreme cold (zone 7+), gas furnaces become more cost-effective **below 25°F**
*   The real comparison is **cost per million BTU**, not price per unit of energy
*   A heat pump with COP 3.0 delivers **300% efficiency** vs the best gas furnace at 98% AFUE
*   Electricity price matters more than most homeowners realize — **check your rate per kWh**
*   Dual-fuel systems combine both for **optimal cost in any climate**

### What You'll Learn

[01 Monthly Operating Cost: Head-to-Head](https://hvaccalculatorhub.com/blog/heat-pump-vs-gas-furnace-operating-cost-comparison#monthly)
 [02 Why Heat Pumps Are More Efficient](https://hvaccalculatorhub.com/blog/heat-pump-vs-gas-furnace-operating-cost-comparison#cop)
 [03 When Gas Furnace Wins: Extreme Cold](https://hvaccalculatorhub.com/blog/heat-pump-vs-gas-furnace-operating-cost-comparison#cold)
 [04 Fuel Price Trends 2026](https://hvaccalculatorhub.com/blog/heat-pump-vs-gas-furnace-operating-cost-comparison#prices)
 [05 Break-Even Point by Climate Zone](https://hvaccalculatorhub.com/blog/heat-pump-vs-gas-furnace-operating-cost-comparison#breakeven)
 [06 Full Winter Annual Cost Analysis](https://hvaccalculatorhub.com/blog/heat-pump-vs-gas-furnace-operating-cost-comparison#annual)
 [07 Dual-Fuel Systems: Best of Both](https://hvaccalculatorhub.com/blog/heat-pump-vs-gas-furnace-operating-cost-comparison#dual)
 [08 Cost Per Hour Comparison](https://hvaccalculatorhub.com/blog/heat-pump-vs-gas-furnace-operating-cost-comparison#hourly)
 [09 Total Cost of Ownership](https://hvaccalculatorhub.com/blog/heat-pump-vs-gas-furnace-operating-cost-comparison#tco)
 [10 Common Mistakes in Cost Comparisons](https://hvaccalculatorhub.com/blog/heat-pump-vs-gas-furnace-operating-cost-comparison#mistakes)
 [11 Real-World Case Studies](https://hvaccalculatorhub.com/blog/heat-pump-vs-gas-furnace-operating-cost-comparison#cases)
 [12 FAQ (8 Questions)](https://hvaccalculatorhub.com/blog/heat-pump-vs-gas-furnace-operating-cost-comparison#faq)

Monthly Operating Cost: Heat Pump vs Gas Furnace Head-to-Head
-------------------------------------------------------------

**The most important table in this entire guide: real monthly heating costs for a typical 2,000 sq ft home across all 7 DOE climate zones, comparing an 8.1 HSPF2 heat pump against a 92% AFUE gas furnace.** These numbers use the national average electricity rate ($0.14/kWh) and natural gas rate ($1.20/therm). Enter your own rates in the calculator above for exact numbers.

| Climate Zone | Example Cities | Annual Heat Load | Heat Pump Monthly | Gas Furnace Monthly | Monthly Winner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Zone 1 | Miami, Phoenix, Honolulu | 20 MBTU | $39 | $27 | Gas by $12 |
| Zone 2 | Houston, Los Angeles, New Orleans | 30 MBTU | $58 | $41 | Gas by $17 |
| Zone 3 | Atlanta, Dallas, Memphis | 40 MBTU | $78 | $54 | Gas by $24 |
| Zone 4 | New York, Kansas City, St. Louis | 55 MBTU | $107 | $75 | Gas by $32 |
| Zone 5 | Chicago, Denver, Indianapolis | 65 MBTU | $127 | $88 | Gas by $39 |
| Zone 6 | Minneapolis, Boston, Burlington | 80 MBTU | $156 | $108 | Gas by $48 |
| Zone 7 | Duluth, Fairbanks, International Falls | 100 MBTU | $218 | $136 | Gas by $82 |

**Important: These Are Average Rates**

At the national average rates ($0.14/kWh electricity, $1.20/therm gas), gas appears cheaper in every zone. But national averages mask enormous regional variation. In the Pacific Northwest (electricity at $0.09/kWh), heat pumps win by 40%+. In the Northeast (gas at $1.80/therm), heat pumps are competitive. The calculator above uses YOUR rates — plug them in for the real answer.

Why Heat Pumps Are More Efficient: COP Explained
------------------------------------------------

**The Coefficient of Performance (COP) is the single number that explains why a heat pump can be cheaper to run than a gas furnace even when electricity costs more per unit than gas.** COP measures how much heat energy a heat pump delivers for each unit of electrical energy it consumes. A COP of 3.0 means the heat pump delivers 3 units of heat for every 1 unit of electricity — an effective 300% efficiency rating.

Compare this to a gas furnace: even the best 98% AFUE furnace converts only 98% of its fuel energy into useful heat. The remaining 2% goes up the flue. An 80% AFUE furnace wastes 20% of every dollar you spend on gas. The heat pump moves heat from outside to inside rather than creating it from scratch, which is why it can exceed 100% efficiency when expressed relative to the electricity it consumes.

#### Heat Pump COP

*   COP 2.5 = Standard efficiency (250%)
*   COP 3.0 = Mid-efficiency (300%)
*   COP 3.5 = High-efficiency (350%)
*   COP 4.0+ = Premium cold-climate models
*   Efficiency decreases as outdoor temp drops

#### Gas Furnace AFUE

*   80% AFUE = Standard (20% waste)
*   92% AFUE = High-efficiency condensing
*   96% AFUE = Premium condensing
*   98% AFUE = Maximum practical efficiency
*   Efficiency stays consistent regardless of outdoor temp

### COP Changes With Outdoor Temperature

A heat pump's COP is not constant — it decreases as outdoor temperatures fall. At 47°F (the standard rating condition), a mid-efficiency heat pump might achieve a COP of 3.0. At 17°F, that same unit might drop to a COP of 2.2. At 0°F, it could fall to 1.8 or lower. This is why heat pump operating costs increase in cold weather — the system works harder and less efficiently to extract heat from colder outdoor air.

Modern cold-climate heat pumps (CCASHPs) maintain higher COP at lower temperatures through enhanced vapor injection (EVI) and inverter-driven compressors. A cold-climate heat pump might maintain a COP of 2.5 at 5°F, compared to 1.5 for a standard unit at the same temperature.

| Outdoor Temp | Standard HP COP | Cold-Climate HP COP | Gas Furnace Effectiveness |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 50°F | 3.5 | 4.0 | Consistent — same as any temp |
| 40°F | 3.0 | 3.5 | Consistent |
| 30°F | 2.5 | 3.0 | Consistent |
| 20°F | 2.0 | 2.6 | Consistent |
| 10°F | 1.7 | 2.2 | Consistent |
| 0°F | 1.4 | 1.9 | Consistent |
| \-10°F | 1.1 | 1.6 | Consistent |

When Gas Furnace Wins: Extreme Cold Climates
--------------------------------------------

**Below approximately 25°F, a gas furnace typically becomes more cost-effective than a standard heat pump in most regions.** This is the temperature where a standard heat pump's COP drops below the break-even point against the local gas price. The exact crossover temperature depends on your electricity and gas rates.

For a homeowner paying $0.14/kWh for electricity and $1.20/therm for gas with a 92% AFUE furnace, the break-even heat pump COP is approximately 2.1. When the outdoor temperature drops low enough that the heat pump's COP falls below 2.1, the gas furnace costs less per unit of heat delivered. For most standard heat pumps, this crossover happens around 25-30°F.

This is why dual-fuel systems exist in cold climates: the heat pump handles the mild-weather heating (where it is cheapest), and the gas furnace takes over during deep cold (where it is cheapest). The system automatically switches at a configured switchover temperature, giving you the lowest possible operating cost regardless of outdoor conditions.

**Zone-Specific Insight**

In Zone 1-2 (Miami, Houston, Los Angeles), temperatures rarely drop below 40°F, so a heat pump is almost always cheaper to run. In Zone 6-7 (Minneapolis, Duluth), temperatures spend weeks below 20°F, making gas the winter workhorse. Zone 4-5 (NYC, Chicago) is where the decision is most nuanced and where the calculator is most valuable.

Fuel Price Trends: Electricity vs Natural Gas 2026
--------------------------------------------------

**The price of electricity and natural gas in your area is the single biggest factor in determining whether a heat pump or gas furnace is cheaper to run.** National averages in 2026: electricity at $0.14/kWh, natural gas at $1.20/therm. But actual rates vary dramatically by state and utility.

| Region | Avg Electricity ($/kWh) | Avg Gas ($/therm) | Heat Pump Favorable? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pacific Northwest (WA, OR) | $0.09-$0.11 | $1.20-$1.50 | Yes — cheap electricity makes HP dominant |
| Mountain West (CO, UT, NV) | $0.11-$0.13 | $0.90-$1.30 | Yes — moderate rates favor HP |
| Southeast (FL, GA, TX) | $0.12-$0.15 | $1.00-$1.40 | Mild climate + moderate rates = HP wins |
| Midwest (OH, IL, MI) | $0.13-$0.16 | $0.80-$1.20 | Depends on gas price — calculator needed |
| Northeast (NY, MA, CT) | $0.18-$0.25 | $1.40-$2.00 | High gas prices make HP competitive |
| California | $0.22-$0.35 | $1.50-$2.00 | Very high electricity — gas often cheaper |

### 2026 Price Trends to Watch

*   **Electricity:** Rising 2-4% annually, driven by grid modernization, renewable integration, and demand growth from EVs and data centers. Time-of-use rates are expanding, creating opportunities for heat pump owners who shift load to off-peak hours.
*   **Natural gas:** Volatile but generally stable in 2026. LNG export demand, winter weather events, and pipeline constraints can cause spikes. The long-term trend is upward as the grid decarbonizes.
*   **The gap is narrowing:** As electricity rates rise and gas prices fluctuate, the operating cost comparison shifts more frequently. This makes the calculator more valuable every year — run it with your actual rates, not assumptions.

The Break-Even Point by Climate Zone
------------------------------------

**The break-even point is the outdoor temperature where a heat pump and gas furnace cost exactly the same to operate.** Above this temperature, the heat pump is cheaper. Below it, the gas furnace is cheaper. The break-even temperature changes with your fuel prices, equipment efficiency, and climate.

For the national average rates ($0.14/kWh, $1.20/therm, 92% AFUE furnace), the break-even COP is approximately 2.1. Looking at the COP table above, this corresponds to approximately 25-30°F for standard heat pumps and 15-20°F for cold-climate heat pumps.

| Electricity Rate | Gas Rate ($1.00/therm) | Gas Rate ($1.50/therm) | Gas Rate ($2.00/therm) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0.10/kWh | COP 1.8 (Below 35°F) | COP 2.6 (Below 20°F) | COP 3.5 (Below 10°F) |
| $0.14/kWh | COP 2.5 (Below 25°F) | COP 3.7 (Below 5°F) | COP 5.0 (HP always wins) |
| $0.18/kWh | COP 3.2 (Below 15°F) | COP 4.8 (HP always wins) | COP 6.4 (HP always wins) |
| $0.25/kWh | COP 4.5 (HP almost always wins) | COP 6.8 (HP always wins) | COP 9.0 (HP always wins) |

Full Winter Annual Cost Analysis
--------------------------------

**Monthly snapshots miss the full picture. The real answer is total annual heating cost, which accounts for the temperature distribution across the entire heating season.** Most heating seasons have many more hours at moderate temperatures than at extreme cold, which favors the heat pump in total annual cost.

For a typical Zone 5 home (Chicago, Denver) with 65 MBTU annual heating load, 8.1 HSPF2 heat pump, and 92% AFUE gas furnace:

| Fuel Rate Scenario | Heat Pump Annual | Gas Furnace Annual | Annual Savings | Winner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0.10/kWh + $1.50/therm | $648 | $1,054 | $406 | Heat pump saves 39% |
| $0.14/kWh + $1.20/therm | $908 | $843 | $65 | Gas saves 7% |
| $0.14/kWh + $1.50/therm | $908 | $1,054 | $146 | Heat pump saves 14% |
| $0.18/kWh + $1.20/therm | $1,167 | $843 | $324 | Gas saves 28% |
| $0.18/kWh + $1.80/therm | $1,167 | $1,265 | $98 | Heat pump saves 8% |
| $0.22/kWh + $1.80/therm | $1,426 | $1,265 | $161 | Gas saves 11% |

**Key Takeaway**

At $0.14/kWh electricity and $1.50/therm gas, a heat pump saves $146/year in Zone 5. At $0.10/kWh and $1.50/therm (Pacific Northwest), the heat pump saves $406/year. The electricity rate is the swing factor — check your actual rate on your utility bill.

Dual-Fuel Systems: Best of Both Worlds
--------------------------------------

**A dual-fuel system combines a heat pump with a gas furnace, using each technology where it is most cost-effective.** The system runs the heat pump when outdoor temperatures are above the economic switchover point (typically 25-35°F) and automatically switches to gas heat when temperatures drop below that point.

The result: the lowest possible annual heating cost regardless of outdoor temperature. The heat pump handles the majority of heating hours (mild weather is far more common than extreme cold), while the gas furnace provides backup during the coldest periods when the heat pump's COP drops below the break-even point.

### How the Switchover Works

1.  The thermostat monitors outdoor temperature via an outdoor sensor.
2.  When outdoor temp is above the configured switchover point, the system runs in heat pump mode.
3.  When outdoor temp drops below the switchover point, the system switches to gas furnace mode.
4.  The switchover temperature is configurable — your installer sets it based on your local fuel prices and equipment performance.
5.  Some systems also switch based on actual COP calculation, not just temperature — optimizing in real time.

### Dual-Fuel Cost Advantage

For a Zone 5 home with $0.14/kWh and $1.20/therm, a dual-fuel system with switchover at 30°F saves approximately 8-15% compared to running either system alone across the full heating season. The savings come from using the heat pump during the ~2,500+ hours above 30°F and the furnace during the ~300-500 hours below 30°F.

Find Your Exact Heating Cost
----------------------------

Use the calculator above with your actual electricity and gas rates to see which system saves you the most money.

[Estimate Full Replacement Cost →](https://hvaccalculatorhub.com/calculator-replacement-cost)

Heat Pump vs Gas Furnace: Cost Per Hour
---------------------------------------

**Understanding hourly operating cost helps you estimate daily and seasonal expenses.** A typical 3-ton heat pump draws approximately 3 kW of electricity during operation, while an 80,000 BTU/hr gas furnace consumes approximately 84,000 BTU/hr of gas input.

| System | Energy Input | Fuel Rate | Cost Per Hour | Heat Delivered |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Heat Pump (COP 3.0) | 3 kW electricity | $0.14/kWh | $0.42 | 30,600 BTU/hr |
| Heat Pump (COP 3.0) | 3 kW electricity | $0.10/kWh | $0.30 | 30,600 BTU/hr |
| Gas Furnace (92% AFUE) | 80,000 BTU/hr input | $1.20/therm | $0.96 | 73,600 BTU/hr |
| Gas Furnace (80% AFUE) | 80,000 BTU/hr input | $1.20/therm | $0.96 | 64,000 BTU/hr |
| Gas Furnace (92% AFUE) | 80,000 BTU/hr input | $1.80/therm | $1.44 | 73,600 BTU/hr |

Note that the heat pump and furnace deliver different amounts of heat per hour. The correct comparison is cost per million BTU delivered, which the calculator's third tab computes for you.

Total Cost of Ownership: Installation + Operating Cost
------------------------------------------------------

**Operating cost is only part of the equation. Total cost of ownership includes equipment purchase, installation, maintenance, repairs, and fuel costs over the system's 15-20 year lifespan.**

| Cost Category | Heat Pump System | Gas Furnace + AC |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Equipment (3-ton) | $5,500-$9,000 | $4,500-$7,500 (furnace) + $4,000-$7,000 (AC) |
| Installation | $2,000-$4,000 | $2,500-$5,000 (both systems) |
| Annual maintenance | $150-$250 | $200-$350 (furnace + AC) |
| Annual operating cost (Zone 5) | $800-$1,200 | $800-$1,100 |
| Typical lifespan | 15-20 years | Furnace: 15-20 yr, AC: 12-15 yr |
| 20-year total cost | $23,000-$34,000 | $28,000-$42,000 |

The heat pump replaces both the furnace and the air conditioner with a single system, reducing total equipment and installation costs. Over 20 years, the combined equipment + operating cost typically favors the heat pump by $5,000-$8,000, even in climates where gas has a marginal operating cost advantage.

Common Mistakes When Comparing Heating Costs
--------------------------------------------

Most homeowners make at least three of these errors when comparing heat pump vs gas furnace costs:

1.  **Comparing fuel prices directly:** Electricity at $0.14/kWh and gas at $1.20/therm are not directly comparable. You must calculate cost per unit of useful heat delivered.
2.  **Ignoring efficiency:** A $0.14/kWh heat pump with COP 3.0 is effectively paying $0.047/kWh for useful heat. A $1.20/therm gas furnace at 92% AFUE is effectively paying $1.30/therm for useful heat.
3.  **Using maximum efficiency all winter:** Heat pump COP changes with outdoor temperature. Using the rated COP (measured at 47°F) for the entire winter overstates efficiency.
4.  **Ignoring fixed utility charges:** Monthly service charges, demand charges, and minimum bills affect total costs.
5.  **Ignoring supplemental heat:** Electric resistance backup (auxiliary/emergency heat) costs 3x more than the heat pump and can significantly increase costs during cold snaps.
6.  **Assuming all heat pumps perform the same:** Equipment efficiency varies from COP 2.5 to COP 4.0+ depending on model, brand, and climate.
7.  **Forgetting cooling:** A heat pump provides both heating and cooling. A gas furnace requires a separate AC system, adding equipment and installation cost.

Real-World Case Studies
-----------------------

### Case 1: Zone 3 Home (Atlanta) — Heat Pump Wins

A 2,200 sq ft home in Atlanta with $0.13/kWh electricity and $1.10/therm gas. Annual heating load: 38 MBTU. The 8.1 HSPF2 heat pump costs approximately $57/month during heating season, while the 92% AFUE gas furnace costs approximately $48/month. Gas is cheaper monthly, but the heat pump also provides cooling — eliminating the need for a separate $4,500 AC unit. The heat pump wins on total cost of ownership by approximately $6,200 over 15 years.

### Case 2: Zone 5 Home (Chicago) — Close Call

A 1,800 sq ft home in Chicago with $0.15/kWh electricity and $1.00/therm gas. Annual heating load: 60 MBTU. The heat pump costs approximately $117/month; the gas furnace costs approximately $68/month. Gas wins monthly by $49. But the heat pump saves $5,000 in installation (no separate AC needed) and costs $200/year less in maintenance. Over 15 years: heat pump total = $26,700; gas + AC total = $29,800. Heat pump wins on total cost by $3,100.

### Case 3: Zone 6 Home (Minneapolis) — Dual-Fuel Optimal

A 2,400 sq ft home in Minneapolis with $0.14/kWh electricity and $1.10/therm gas. Annual heating load: 85 MBTU. Pure heat pump: $172/month. Pure gas: $116/month. Dual-fuel with switchover at 30°F: $108/month average (heat pump above 30°F, gas below). The dual-fuel system costs $8 less per month than pure gas while eliminating the separate AC system. Best of both worlds.

Maintenance Costs: Heat Pump vs Gas Furnace
-------------------------------------------

Heat pump maintenance is generally less expensive because there is one system to maintain instead of two (furnace + AC). A heat pump tune-up runs $150-$250 per visit, while maintaining both a furnace and AC costs $200-$350 per year. The heat pump also has no combustion components (no heat exchanger, no flue, no gas valve), which eliminates the annual combustion safety inspection that gas furnaces require.

Environmental Impact Comparison
-------------------------------

A heat pump produces zero direct emissions at the point of use. Its indirect emissions depend on the electricity grid mix. On the U.S. average grid (approximately 0.4 kg CO2/kWh), a heat pump with COP 3.0 produces roughly 2.3 lbs CO2 per 100,000 BTU. A 92% AFUE gas furnace produces approximately 11.7 lbs CO2 per 100,000 BTU — about 5x more. Even on a coal-heavy grid, the heat pump typically produces less CO2 than a gas furnace.

Future Fuel Price Projections 2026-2030
---------------------------------------

Electricity prices are projected to rise 2-4% annually through 2030, driven by grid modernization, renewable integration, and demand growth. Natural gas prices are more volatile but generally trending upward due to LNG export demand and pipeline constraints. The net effect: the operating cost gap between heat pumps and gas furnaces will narrow in many regions, making the heat pump's total cost advantage more pronounced over time.

Decision Matrix: Heat Pump vs Gas Furnace
-----------------------------------------

| Factor | Choose Heat Pump If... | Choose Gas Furnace If... |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Climate | Zones 1-4 (mild to moderate winters) | Zones 6-7 (extreme cold) |
| Electricity rate | Below $0.15/kWh | Above $0.20/kWh with cheap gas |
| Gas rate | Above $1.50/therm | Below $1.00/therm |
| Existing infrastructure | No gas line, or want single system | Existing gas line + furnace |
| Cooling needed | Yes — HP provides both heating and cooling | No — or gas furnace with separate AC |
| Environmental priority | Zero direct emissions, lower CO2 | Lower priority |
| Best overall value | Total cost of ownership over 15+ years | Lowest monthly gas bill in cold climates |

Glossary and Technical Reference
--------------------------------

| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| COP (Coefficient of Performance) | Ratio of heat delivered to electrical energy consumed. COP 3.0 = 300% effective efficiency. |
| HSPF2 (Heating Seasonal Performance Factor 2) | Seasonal average heating efficiency for heat pumps. Higher = more efficient. Range: 7.5-13+. |
| AFUE (Annual Fuel Utilization Efficiency) | Percentage of fuel energy converted to useful heat. 92% AFUE = 92% efficient. |
| Break-even COP | The COP at which a heat pump costs the same to run as a gas furnace at given fuel prices. |
| Dual-fuel system | Combines a heat pump with a gas furnace, switching between them based on outdoor temperature. |
| Economic balance point | The outdoor temperature where heat pump and gas furnace operating costs are equal. |
| MBTU | One million BTU — the standard unit for comparing heating energy across fuel types. |
| Therm | 100,000 BTU of natural gas energy content. |
| Time-of-use rates | Electricity pricing that varies by time of day, potentially favoring heat pumps with smart scheduling. |
| Auxiliary/emergency heat | Electric resistance backup in a heat pump system. Costs 3x more than heat pump mode. |

Complete Resource Directory
---------------------------

*   [HVAC Replacement Cost Calculator](https://hvaccalculatorhub.com/calculator-replacement-cost)
     — estimate the full installed cost of a new heat pump or furnace system.
*   [Energy Cost Calculator](https://hvaccalculatorhub.com/calculator-energy)
     — compare annual energy costs across heating systems.
*   [BTU Calculator](https://hvaccalculatorhub.com/calculator-btu)
     — size your heating system correctly.
*   [Repair vs Replace Tool](https://hvaccalculatorhub.com/calculator-repair-replace)
     — the $5,000 rule calculator.
*   [Regional HVAC Costs by State](https://hvaccalculatorhub.com/blog/regional-hvac-costs-by-state)
     — local pricing data for every state.
*   [2026 HVAC Tax Credits Guide](https://hvaccalculatorhub.com/blog/2026-hvac-tax-credits-guide)
     — Section 25C credits up to $2,000 for heat pumps.
*   [Find a Contractor](https://hvaccalculatorhub.com/find-contractor)
     — get quotes from certified HVAC professionals.

Heat Pump Electricity Consumption: How to Read Your Bill
--------------------------------------------------------

**Understanding how a heat pump affects your electricity bill requires knowing both the power draw and the runtime.** A typical 3-ton heat pump has a compressor that draws 2.5-4.5 kW depending on the outdoor temperature and whether it is running at full capacity or modulating down via an inverter. At $0.14/kWh, running a 3 kW compressor for 8 hours costs approximately $3.36. That same compressor, running at COP 3.0, delivers 81,600 BTU of heat — enough to maintain a 1,500 sq ft home in Zone 4 conditions for about 8 hours.

### Understanding Heat Pump Runtime

Unlike a gas furnace that cycles on and off at full capacity, modern inverter-driven heat pumps run at variable speeds, modulating their output to match the heating load. This means they run for longer periods at lower power levels, which is actually more efficient. A heat pump might run continuously at 40% capacity rather than cycling on at 100% and off at 0%. The total electricity consumption depends on the integrated power draw over the entire heating season, not just peak power.

| Heat Pump Size | Typical Power Draw | Electricity per Hour | Cost per Hour ($0.14/kWh) | Cost per Hour ($0.10/kWh) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2-ton (24,000 BTU) | 1.8-2.8 kW | 1.8-2.8 kWh | $0.25-$0.39 | $0.18-$0.28 |
| 3-ton (36,000 BTU) | 2.5-4.0 kW | 2.5-4.0 kWh | $0.35-$0.56 | $0.25-$0.40 |
| 4-ton (48,000 BTU) | 3.2-5.2 kW | 3.2-5.2 kWh | $0.45-$0.73 | $0.32-$0.52 |
| 5-ton (60,000 BTU) | 4.0-6.5 kW | 4.0-6.5 kWh | $0.56-$0.91 | $0.40-$0.65 |

Gas Furnace Consumption: Reading the Gas Meter
----------------------------------------------

**A gas furnace's fuel consumption is straightforward: multiply the input BTU rating by runtime and divide by the AFUE to get useful heat output.** An 80,000 BTU/hr input furnace at 92% AFUE delivers 73,600 BTU/hr of useful heat. At $1.20/therm, running this furnace for 8 hours consumes 6.7 therms, costing approximately $8.04. That delivers 588,800 BTU of heat — more than a heat pump can deliver in the same time, which is why furnaces dominate during extreme cold when heating loads are highest.

### Gas Furnace Sizing vs Actual Load

Most gas furnaces are oversized for the actual heating load. A typical 2,000 sq ft home in Zone 5 needs approximately 60,000-80,000 BTU/hr of heating capacity at design conditions (the coldest day of the year), but the average winter day only requires 30,000-45,000 BTU/hr. Modern two-stage and modulating furnaces can throttle down to match the actual load, improving efficiency. A single-stage furnace running at full capacity for 8 hours may use more gas than a modulating furnace that runs at 50% for most of those hours.

**Why This Matters for Cost Comparison**

A gas furnace that is oversized for the home wastes fuel through short-cycling. A properly sized heat pump with inverter technology modulates to match the load exactly. This is one reason real-world heat pump efficiency often exceeds the rated COP — inverter heat pumps spend most of their runtime at partial load where they are most efficient.

Cold Climate Heat Pumps: Performance Below 25°F
-----------------------------------------------

**Cold-climate air-source heat pumps (ccASHPs) have transformed the economics of heat pump heating in northern climates.** These systems use enhanced vapor injection (EVI), twin rotary or scroll compressors, and advanced defrost controls to maintain meaningful heating capacity and efficiency well below 0°F. While a standard heat pump might lose 50-60% of its rated capacity at 17°F, a cold-climate unit maintains 75-85% of rated capacity.

### How Cold-Climate Heat Pumps Work Differently

1.  **Enhanced Vapor Injection (EVI):** A second scroll or piston stage injects additional refrigerant vapor into the compressor at low temperatures, maintaining compression ratio and capacity.
2.  **Inverter-driven compressors:** Variable-speed compressors can run at very high speeds during extreme cold, pushing more refrigerant through the system to extract maximum heat from cold outdoor air.
3.  **Intelligent defrost:** Advanced defrost algorithms minimize the energy penalty of periodic defrost cycles, which can waste 10-15% of heating energy in standard units.
4.  **Extended operating range:** Cold-climate heat pumps are rated and certified for operation down to -13°F or lower, compared to 5-15°F for standard units.

| Outdoor Temp | Standard HP Capacity | CC-HP Capacity | Standard COP | CC-HP COP | Gas Furnace Output |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 47°F (rated) | 36,000 BTU/hr | 40,000 BTU/hr | 3.2 | 3.8 | 73,600 BTU/hr |
| 30°F | 28,800 BTU/hr | 35,200 BTU/hr | 2.5 | 3.2 | 73,600 BTU/hr |
| 17°F | 21,600 BTU/hr | 30,400 BTU/hr | 2.0 | 2.7 | 73,600 BTU/hr |
| 5°F | 14,400 BTU/hr | 25,600 BTU/hr | 1.6 | 2.3 | 73,600 BTU/hr |
| \-5°F | 7,200 BTU/hr | 20,800 BTU/hr | 1.2 | 1.9 | 73,600 BTU/hr |
| \-13°F | Not rated | 16,000 BTU/hr | N/A | 1.6 | 73,600 BTU/hr |

State-by-State: Heat Pump Operating Cost Comparison
---------------------------------------------------

**Your state's average electricity and gas rates determine which system is cheaper to run.** The table below shows the annual heating cost for a Zone 4 home (55 MBTU load) with an 8.1 HSPF2 heat pump vs a 92% AFUE gas furnace, using actual 2026 state average rates.

| State | Elec Rate | Gas Rate | HP Annual Cost | Gas Annual Cost | Winner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Washington | $0.09 | $1.30 | $574 | $776 | HP saves $202 |
| Oregon | $0.10 | $1.20 | $638 | $716 | HP saves $78 |
| Colorado | $0.11 | $1.10 | $702 | $656 | Gas saves $46 |
| Florida | $0.12 | $1.30 | $765 | $776 | HP saves $11 |
| Texas | $0.12 | $1.10 | $765 | $656 | Gas saves $109 |
| Georgia | $0.12 | $1.20 | $765 | $716 | Gas saves $49 |
| Illinois | $0.14 | $1.00 | $893 | $593 | Gas saves $300 |
| Ohio | $0.13 | $1.10 | $829 | $656 | Gas saves $173 |
| New York | $0.19 | $1.50 | $1,207 | $890 | Gas saves $317 |
| Massachusetts | $0.22 | $1.60 | $1,398 | $949 | Gas saves $449 |
| California | $0.27 | $1.70 | $1,716 | $1,009 | Gas saves $707 |
| New Hampshire | $0.20 | $1.80 | $1,270 | $1,068 | Gas saves $202 |

**These Are National Averages — Your Rates May Differ**

State averages hide utility-level variation. In California, PG&E customers pay $0.35/kWh while SMUD customers pay $0.12/kWh. In New York, Con Edison customers pay $0.25/kWh while NYSEG customers pay $0.15/kWh. Always check your actual utility bill for the per-kWh and per-therm rates.

Advantages of Heat Pumps Over Gas Furnaces
------------------------------------------

*   **Dual functionality:** Provides both heating and cooling in one system, eliminating the need for a separate AC unit ($4,000-$7,000 savings).
*   **Higher effective efficiency:** COP 2.5-4.0+ translates to 250-400% effective efficiency, vs maximum 98% AFUE for the best gas furnace.
*   **Lower maintenance:** One system to maintain instead of two. No combustion components, no heat exchanger to crack, no flue to inspect.
*   **Zero direct emissions:** No on-site combustion, no carbon monoxide risk, no gas line required.
*   **Zone compatibility:** In zones 1-4, heat pumps are typically the most cost-effective heating and cooling solution.
*   **Time-of-use optimization:** Smart thermostats can shift heat pump runtime to off-peak electricity hours, reducing costs further.
*   **Grid compatibility:** Heat pumps pair well with rooftop solar, battery storage, and time-of-use rate structures.

Advantages of Gas Furnaces Over Heat Pumps
------------------------------------------

*   **Consistent performance:** AFUE stays constant regardless of outdoor temperature — a 92% furnace delivers the same efficiency at -10°F as at 40°F.
*   **Lower operating cost in cold climates:** In zones 5-7, gas is often cheaper to run during the coldest months when heat pump COP drops below 2.0.
*   **Higher capacity:** A gas furnace can deliver 80,000-120,000 BTU/hr of continuous heat, more than most residential heat pumps.
*   **Existing infrastructure:** If you already have a gas line and furnace, the marginal cost of continuing to use gas is lower than converting to a heat pump.
*   **Rapid heating:** Gas furnaces deliver full-capacity heat almost immediately, warming a cold house faster than a heat pump at low COP.
*   **No electrical upgrade:** Gas furnaces require only a standard 120V circuit, while large heat pumps may require a 240V circuit upgrade.

Heat Pump + Solar: The Ultimate Operating Cost Reduction
--------------------------------------------------------

**Pairing a heat pump with rooftop solar panels can reduce your heating operating cost to near zero.** A 6 kW solar array in most US locations generates 7,000-10,000 kWh per year — enough to offset 50-80% of a heat pump's annual electricity consumption in zones 3-5. With net metering, excess summer production credits winter consumption, further reducing your annual electricity cost.

The economics are compelling: a heat pump at COP 3.0 powered by solar electricity at $0.02/kWh (the effective cost of solar electricity over its 25-year life) delivers heat at approximately $0.68 per million BTU — roughly one-twentieth the cost of gas heating. Even without full solar offset, a heat pump owner with a 50% solar offset pays half the operating cost of a gas furnace owner.

How Home Insulation Affects the Comparison
------------------------------------------

**A well-insulated home reduces heating demand, which benefits both systems but disproportionately benefits the heat pump.** Here is why: a well-insulated home has a lower peak heating load, meaning the heat pump rarely needs to run at full capacity. At partial load, the heat pump operates at higher COP. A poorly insulated home with high peak demand may push the heat pump into defrost cycles and low-COP territory more often, narrowing or eliminating the operating cost advantage.

| Insulation Level | Annual Heat Load (Zone 5) | HP Annual Cost | Gas Annual Cost | HP Savings |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Poor (R-13 walls, R-19 attic) | 85 MBTU | $1,412 | $1,003 | Gas saves $409 |
| Average (R-19 walls, R-30 attic) | 65 MBTU | $1,080 | $770 | Gas saves $310 |
| Good (R-21 walls, R-49 attic) | 45 MBTU | $748 | $532 | Gas saves $216 |
| Excellent (R-30 walls, R-60 attic) | 30 MBTU | $499 | $355 | Gas saves $144 |

At national average rates, gas remains cheaper in every insulation scenario for Zone 5. But improve the insulation AND lower the electricity rate (to $0.10/kWh, which is the Pacific Northwest average), and the heat pump wins in every scenario.

Tax Credits and Rebates: How They Change the Math
-------------------------------------------------

**Federal Section 25C tax credits and utility rebates can offset the higher upfront cost of a heat pump system, making the total cost of ownership significantly more favorable.**

| Incentive | Heat Pump Credit | Gas Furnace Credit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Section 25C (Federal) | Up to $2,000 (30% of project cost) | Up to $600 (AFUE 97%+) |
| Utility rebates (typical) | $500-$2,000 (varies by utility) | $100-$400 (high-efficiency) |
| State rebates (varies) | $500-$3,000 (some states) | $0-$200 (limited) |
| Total potential savings | $1,000-$7,000 | $100-$1,200 |

The combined federal credit and utility rebates can offset $1,500-$4,000 of the heat pump's equipment premium, making it cost-competitive with a gas furnace even before considering operating costs.

Time-of-Use Electricity Rates: Hidden Heat Pump Advantage
---------------------------------------------------------

**Many utilities offer time-of-use (TOU) electricity rates where off-peak electricity costs 40-60% less than peak rates.** A smart thermostat can schedule the heat pump to run primarily during off-peak hours (typically 9 PM to 7 AM), pre-heating the home before peak rates begin. This strategy can reduce the heat pump's effective electricity rate by 20-30%, making it significantly more competitive against gas.

For example, if your TOU rates are $0.08/kWh off-peak and $0.22/kWh peak, a heat pump running 70% during off-peak hours has an effective rate of approximately $0.122/kWh — lower than the standard flat rate of $0.14/kWh. At this effective rate, the heat pump's operating cost advantage increases substantially.

Geothermal Heat Pumps: The Ultimate Operating Cost
--------------------------------------------------

**Geothermal (ground-source) heat pumps achieve COP of 4.0-5.0+ by exchanging heat with the ground rather than outdoor air.** Because ground temperatures remain relatively stable (50-60°F year-round), geothermal systems maintain high efficiency even during the coldest winter days. A geothermal system in Zone 5 can cost $400-$600 per year to heat a 2,000 sq ft home — roughly half the operating cost of an air-source heat pump and a third of a gas furnace.

The tradeoff: geothermal systems have a much higher upfront cost ($15,000-$30,000 installed including the ground loop), but they last 25-50 years with minimal maintenance. Over a 25-year lifespan, the total cost of ownership can favor geothermal by $10,000-$20,000 compared to any air-source or combustion system.

Smart Thermostat Strategies for Heat Pump Owners
------------------------------------------------

**A smart thermostat can reduce heat pump operating costs by 10-15% through optimized scheduling, learning, and integration with utility rate structures.** Key strategies:

1.  **Setback during unoccupied hours:** Reducing the setpoint by 3-5°F when the home is empty for 4+ hours. The heat pump's inverter ramp-up is gradual, so set back less aggressively than with a gas furnace.

NEWS

Federal and State HVAC Rebate Programs
======================================

Published April 20, 2026Updated April 20, 20267 min readNews

[HVAC rebates](https://hvacdatabase.com/us/articles/?topic=hvac-rebates)
[federal tax credits](https://hvacdatabase.com/us/articles/?topic=federal-tax-credits)
[heat pump incentives](https://hvacdatabase.com/us/articles/?topic=heat-pump-incentives)
[energy efficiency](https://hvacdatabase.com/us/articles/?topic=energy-efficiency)
[utility rebates](https://hvacdatabase.com/us/articles/?topic=utility-rebates)
[homeowner savings](https://hvacdatabase.com/us/articles/?topic=homeowner-savings)
[SEER2](https://hvacdatabase.com/us/articles/?topic=seer2)
[HSPF2](https://hvacdatabase.com/us/articles/?topic=hspf2)

A practical guide to claiming federal tax credits and state/utility rebates for energy-efficient HVAC. Includes eligibility tables, checklists, and links to our rebate finder.

![Federal and State HVAC Rebate Programs](https://hvacdatabase.com/generated/article-ductless-living-room-07.png)

Clear Stance

Clear Recommendation
--------------------

For most homeowners, a high-efficiency heat pump offers the best rebate value and long-term energy savings. In very cold climates, consider a dual-fuel system. Always verify local incentives before buying.

What Matters Most
-----------------

*   Federal tax credits cover up to 30% of costs, capped at $2,000 for heat pumps.
*   State and utility rebates can add thousands in instant savings.
*   Efficiency thresholds are strict—check SEER2, HSPF2, or AFUE ratings before purchase.
*   Hire a licensed contractor and keep all documentation for claims.
*   Combine incentives with home weatherization for maximum return.

Strengths
---------

*   Heat pumps provide heating and cooling in one unit, reducing fuel reliance.
*   Tax credits are available for multiple years, allowing phased upgrades.
*   Immediate rebates lower the upfront cost barrier.
*   High efficiency leads to lower monthly bills and increased comfort.

Weaknesses
----------

*   In extremely cold areas without backup, some heat pumps may struggle (though cold-climate models have improved).
*   Rebate availability varies by state and utility funding, leading to uncertainty.
*   High-efficiency equipment often costs more upfront, even after incentives.
*   Paperwork can be complex, requiring tax filing adjustments.

Decision Summary: Which HVAC Upgrade Path Saves More?
-----------------------------------------------------

| Scenario | Usually do | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| You live in a moderate climate, current system >10 years old | Replace with ENERGY STAR heat pump | Maximizes federal credit ($2,000) and qualifies for most state rebates; lower operating cost. |
| You have an older furnace and AC, and natural gas is cheap | Install a high-AFUE gas furnace and efficient AC | Lower upfront cost with simpler installation, but rebates are smaller ($600 each). |
| Your ductwork is leaky or non-existent | Consider ductless mini-split heat pump | Avoids costly ductwork, high efficiency, and full credit eligibility. |
| You rent or plan to move soon | Prioritize smart thermostat and minor weatherization | Low investment, but still some utility rebates. |

Quick Answer: How to Save on Your HVAC Upgrade
----------------------------------------------

You can slash HVAC costs by stacking federal tax credits, state rebates, and utility incentives. The average homeowner saves $2,000–$8,000 on a qualifying system. Key steps:

1.  Use our [Rebate Finder](https://hvacdatabase.com/us/tools/rebate-finder)
     to see local offers.
2.  Choose equipment meeting minimum SEER2/HSPF2 thresholds (see table below).
3.  Hire a licensed pro and keep receipts. Credits reduce taxes; rebates give cash back. Act soon—some programs have limited funds or phase-out dates.

Do You Qualify? Federal Tax Credit Eligibility & Decision Rules
---------------------------------------------------------------

To claim the full credit, your new system must meet or exceed these 2024–2032 requirements. State and utility rebates often align but may have stricter thresholds—always verify with our [Rebate Finder](https://hvacdatabase.com/us/tools/rebate-finder)
.

| Equipment Type | Minimum Efficiency Requirement | Maximum Federal Credit | Key Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ducted Heat Pump | SEER2 ≥ 15.2, HSPF2 ≥ 8.1 | $2,000 | Must meet CEE highest tier; covers split systems and packaged units |
| Ductless Mini-Split Heat Pump | SEER2 ≥ 16, HSPF2 ≥ 9.5 | $2,000 | Ideal for homes without existing ductwork |
| Central Air Conditioner | SEER2 ≥ 16 | $600 | ENERGY STAR Most Efficient designation required |
| Gas Furnace | AFUE ≥ 97% | $600 | Only for high-efficiency models; limited to 30% of cost |
| Heat Pump Water Heater | UEF ≥ 3.5 | $2,000 | Replaces electric resistance water heater; credit shared with heat pump |

**Decision Rules:** If your heating load is over 40,000 BTU/hr and you live in a cold climate (below 5°F design temperature), pair a heat pump with a gas furnace (dual-fuel) to maximize rebates and comfort. For cooling-dominant regions, prioritize SEER2 over HSPF2. Check our [BTU Calculator](https://hvacdatabase.com/us/tools/btu-calculator)
 to size your system correctly.

Safety Boundaries: What You Can (and Cannot) Do Yourself
--------------------------------------------------------

While claiming rebates is paperwork, installing HVAC equipment involves high-voltage electricity, refrigerant, and combustion gases. As a homeowner, you can:

*   Compare quotes and verify contractor licenses using our [contractor comparison tool](https://hvacdatabase.com/us/compare-contractors)
    .
*   Verify equipment model numbers against approved lists from the manufacturer’s AHRI certificate.
*   Fill out rebate forms and attach required documentation.

**Never attempt:**

*   Installing or repairing refrigerant lines (requires EPA certification).
*   Connecting gas lines or modifying combustion vents.
*   Replacing capacitors, contactors, compressors, or control boards.
*   Modifying electrical panels or running high-voltage wiring.

Always hire a [licensed, insured professional](https://hvacdatabase.com/us/search)
 for installation. Your safety and warranty coverage depend on it.

Use Our Free Tools to Maximize Your Savings
-------------------------------------------

Take the guesswork out of rebate hunting:

*   [**Rebate Finder**](https://hvacdatabase.com/us/tools/rebate-finder)
     – Enter your ZIP to see all federal, state, and utility incentives you qualify for.
*   [**HVAC Cost Estimator**](https://hvacdatabase.com/us/tools/cost-estimator)
     – Compare installed prices before and after incentives.
*   [**Energy Savings Calculator**](https://hvacdatabase.com/us/tools/energy-calculator)
     – See how much a high-efficiency system could cut your monthly bills.
*   [**Repair or Replace Calculator**](https://hvacdatabase.com/us/tools/repair-or-replace)
     – Not sure if you need a new system? This tool helps you decide.

Contractor Checklist: 7 Questions Before You Sign
-------------------------------------------------

1.  **Licensing & Insurance:** "Are you licensed, bonded, and insured in this state? May I see proof?"
2.  **Rebate Eligibility:** "Will this exact model number qualify for the federal tax credit and all local rebates? Please put that in writing."
3.  **Paperwork Handling:** "Do you file the utility rebate on my behalf, or do I submit it?"
4.  **Load Calculation:** "Can you provide a Manual J load calculation to properly size the equipment? (Required for most rebates.)"
5.  **Warranties:** "What are the equipment and labor warranties? Do they meet rebate program requirements?"
6.  **Experience:** "How many of these specific units have you installed in the past year? Can I speak with a recent customer?"
7.  **Total Price Breakdown:** "Please itemize equipment, labor, permits, and any disposal fees. Will the rebate be deducted upfront?"

Local Market Considerations
---------------------------

Your location shapes which incentives are best and what equipment makes sense.

### Hot & Dry (Southwest)

Prioritize high-SEER2 air conditioners or heat pumps with enhanced dehumidification. Some Arizona utilities offer extra rebates for solar-ready heat pumps. Find a [Phoenix AC contractor](https://hvacdatabase.com/hvac-contractors/phoenix-az/ac-repair)
 familiar with local rebates.

### Cold & Snowy (Northeast, Midwest)

Cold-climate heat pumps (rated to -15°F) now qualify for full credits. In older homes, pair with [air sealing](https://hvacdatabase.com/us/articles/how-to-seal-air-leaks-in-your-home)
 and insulation. A dual-fuel system (heat pump + high-efficiency gas furnace) can provide backup and still earn partial credits. Check our [Chicago heating contractor](https://hvacdatabase.com/hvac-contractors/chicago-il/heating-repair)
 list for pros who understand cold-weather performance.

### Hot & Humid (Southeast, Gulf Coast)

Variable-speed systems dramatically improve humidity control. Look for rebates tied to ENERGY STAR HVAC with integrated dehumidification. [Get a home energy audit](https://hvacdatabase.com/us/articles/how-to-get-a-home-energy-audit)
 before upgrading—duct leakage is common.

### Coastal (Salt Air Exposure)

Salt corrosion shortens coil life. Choose equipment with coastal warranties (e.g., factory-applied anti-corrosion coatings). Some rebates require corrosion-resistant models; check with local utilities.

### Older Homes (Pre-1980)

Many older homes need electrical panel upgrades or duct sealing before a new HVAC can be installed. Programs often bundle [weatherization incentives](https://hvacdatabase.com/us/articles/how-to-seal-air-leaks-in-your-home)
. Use our [Cost Estimator](https://hvacdatabase.com/us/tools/cost-estimator)
 to budget for any necessary prep work.

Methodology: How We Calculate Savings Estimates
-----------------------------------------------

Our cost ranges and savings projections are editorial estimates based on national average installation prices, manufacturer rebate data, and public utility filings. Actual rebate amounts vary by ZIP code, equipment model, household income (for some state programs), and program fund availability. We update this guide quarterly or when major policy changes occur. Always confirm current details with your contractor and official program websites before purchase.

Frequently Asked Questions
--------------------------

### Can I combine federal tax credits with state rebates and utility incentives?

Yes, in most cases. Federal credits are applied to your income tax, while state and utility rebates are cash paid directly. You can often stack them, but some state programs may reduce the eligible cost for the federal credit. Generally, the full installed cost qualifies for the credit, even if a rebate reduced your out-of-pocket expense. Consult a tax professional, but stacking is the norm.

### What if my contractor isn’t familiar with rebates?

Choose a contractor who regularly participates in efficiency programs. Ask them to provide the AHRI certificate for your equipment to prove eligibility. If they can’t, use our [contractor search](https://hvacdatabase.com/us/search)
 to find a vetted pro in your area who knows the rebate landscape.

### Do renters qualify for HVAC rebates?

Typically, no, because the property owner must install the system. However, renters can sometimes receive rebates for [smart thermostats](https://hvacdatabase.com/us/articles/how-to-use-ceiling-fans-to-boost-hvac-efficiency)
 or minor weatherization. Talk to your landlord about available incentives—they may be willing to upgrade if you share the savings.

### How long do rebates and credits last?

Federal credits (25C) are in effect through December 31, 2032, with no sign of early expiration. State and utility rebates vary: some are ongoing annual programs, while others have limited funding that runs out quickly. We recommend checking our [Rebate Finder](https://hvacdatabase.com/us/tools/rebate-finder)
 monthly for real-time availability.

### I installed an efficient system last year. Can I still claim the credit?

Yes, for installations placed in service after 2021, you can claim the federal credit on your current or amended tax return. You’ll need the manufacturer’s certification statement and your itemized invoice. Keep these for your records in case of audit. The credit is retroactive to 2022 installations.

Building Performance & Envelope

August 30, 2024 · Updated July 26, 2026

Gas Furnace Performance in Very Cold Climates
=============================================

Table of Contents
-----------------

When temperatures plummet well below zero, a gas furnace faces its ultimate test. The difference between a system that keeps a home comfortable and one that struggles to maintain 60°F often comes down to design choices that are invisible to the average homeowner. For technicians working in very cold climates—where winter design temperatures can hit -20°F or lower—understanding how a gas furnace actually performs under extreme load is essential for proper sizing, installation, and troubleshooting.

What Defines a Gas Furnace’s Performance in Extreme Cold
--------------------------------------------------------

Furnace performance in very cold climates is not simply about whether the unit can produce heat. It is about how efficiently and reliably it can convert fuel into usable heat while overcoming the increased heat loss of the building envelope. The key metric here is the **heating capacity** at the outdoor design temperature, which must match or slightly exceed the home’s calculated heat loss.

In moderate climates, a furnace might cycle on and off frequently, running at partial load for much of the season. In extreme cold, however, the furnace often runs continuously or in very long cycles. This changes the dynamics of heat exchanger temperature, flue gas condensation, and even the wear on components like the inducer motor and gas valve. A furnace that performs adequately at 20°F may fail to keep up at -20°F if it was sized based on average rather than extreme conditions.

### The Role of AFUE in Cold Weather

Annual Fuel Utilization Efficiency (AFUE) is a laboratory rating that assumes steady-state operation under specific conditions. In very cold weather, a condensing furnace (90%+ AFUE) can actually lose some efficiency because the incoming combustion air is so cold that it chills the heat exchanger surfaces, potentially causing excessive condensation or even freezing of the condensate drain. Non-condensing furnaces (80% AFUE) avoid this issue but waste more heat up the flue.

For technicians, the practical takeaway is that a 96% AFUE furnace does not deliver 96% efficiency when the outdoor temperature is -10°F and the unit is cycling on a cold start. The actual seasonal efficiency in extreme climates may be 2–4% lower than the rated AFUE due to off-design conditions.

Critical Design Features for Very Cold Climates
-----------------------------------------------

Not all gas furnaces are built to handle extreme cold. Manufacturers offer specific models or options for northern climates, and knowing what to look for can prevent callbacks and frozen pipes.

### Sealed Combustion vs. Natural Draft

In very cold climates, **sealed combustion** (direct vent) furnaces are strongly preferred. These units draw combustion air from outside through a dedicated PVC pipe, rather than pulling cold, dry air from the basement or crawlspace. Natural draft furnaces, which rely on indoor air for combustion, can create negative pressure in the home, pulling in more cold air through cracks and increasing heat loss. Sealed combustion also prevents the risk of backdrafting when exhaust fans (bathroom, kitchen, or dryer) are running.

### Condensate Management Below Freezing

Condensing furnaces produce acidic condensate that must drain away. In extreme cold, the condensate drain line can freeze if it runs through an unheated space or if the drain trap is not properly insulated. Technicians should install the drain line with a minimum 1/4-inch per foot slope, use PVC or CPVC that can handle the acidity, and consider heat tape on exposed sections. Some manufacturers now offer condensate drain heaters or recommend routing the drain through a heated floor drain.

A frozen condensate line will cause the furnace to shut down on a pressure switch fault, often leading to a no-heat call in the middle of a cold snap. This is one of the most common service issues in very cold climates.

### Heat Exchanger Material and Design

Standard aluminized steel heat exchangers can handle normal temperature swings, but extreme cold can cause more rapid thermal expansion and contraction. Stainless steel primary or secondary heat exchangers are more resistant to thermal stress and corrosion from acidic condensate. For technicians, checking the heat exchanger type during installation or replacement is critical—a lower-cost unit with an aluminized steel exchanger may fail prematurely in a very cold climate.

Sizing Considerations for Extreme Cold
--------------------------------------

Proper furnace sizing is arguably the most important factor for performance in very cold climates. An oversized furnace will short-cycle, never reaching steady-state efficiency, and will fail to dehumidify the home properly. An undersized furnace will run continuously and still not maintain setpoint on the coldest days.

### Manual J Load Calculation Is Non-Negotiable

In very cold climates, a rule-of-thumb sizing approach is unacceptable. Technicians must perform a full **Manual J load calculation** that accounts for:

*   Insulation levels in walls, attic, and floors
*   Window U-values and solar heat gain
*   Air infiltration rates (blower door test recommended)
*   Duct losses in unconditioned spaces
*   Internal heat gains from occupants and appliances

The design temperature should be the 99% or 99.6% winter design temperature from ASHRAE data for the specific location. Using a warmer design temperature will result in an undersized furnace that cannot keep up during extreme cold events.

### The 140% Rule and Its Limits

Some contractors use the “140% rule,” sizing the furnace at 140% of the calculated heat loss. This provides a safety margin for extreme cold snaps and recovery from setback. However, in very cold climates, this margin can lead to oversizing if the heat loss calculation is already conservative. A better approach is to size the furnace to match the heat loss at the design temperature, then verify that the furnace’s minimum output (if modulating) is low enough to prevent short-cycling in milder weather.

For two-stage or modulating furnaces, the low-stage output should be at or below 65% of the design heat loss to avoid short-cycling during shoulder seasons. This is a common mistake—installing a modulating furnace with a high minimum firing rate that never actually runs in low stage.

Common Performance Issues in Very Cold Climates
-----------------------------------------------

Even a properly sized and installed furnace can develop problems when temperatures drop to extreme lows. Technicians should be aware of these failure modes.

### Flue Gas Condensation in Non-Condensing Furnaces

Non-condensing furnaces (80% AFUE) are designed to keep flue gas temperatures above 140°F to prevent condensation in the chimney or vent. In very cold weather, the vent pipe can cool the flue gas below the dew point, causing acidic condensation that can corrode metal vents or damage masonry chimneys. This is especially common with sidewall venting or long horizontal runs. Technicians should inspect vent pipes for signs of corrosion or water staining and consider upgrading to a condensing furnace if this is a recurring issue.

### Pressure Switch Faults from Wind and Snow

High winds can create pressure imbalances that cause the pressure switch to open, shutting down the furnace. Snow can block intake or exhaust vents, leading to the same result. In very cold climates, technicians should ensure that vent terminations are located above the expected snow line (typically 12–24 inches above the roof or grade) and are not subject to wind tunneling from building corners. Some manufacturers offer wind-resistant vent caps for extreme conditions.

### Gas Pressure and Supply Issues

Natural gas pressure can drop during extreme cold events because of increased demand across the grid. Propane systems are especially vulnerable, as propane vapor pressure decreases in cold weather, leading to insufficient gas flow. Technicians should verify manifold gas pressure at the furnace during peak demand and check that the propane tank is sized for the expected load. A 500-gallon tank may be insufficient for a large home in a very cold climate if the furnace runs continuously for days.

Installation Best Practices for Extreme Cold
--------------------------------------------

Getting the installation right from the start prevents most cold-weather performance issues. These practices should be standard for any furnace installed in a very cold climate.

### Combustion Air Intake Location

For sealed combustion furnaces, the intake must be located away from sources of snow, ice, and exhaust from other appliances. A common mistake is placing the intake too close to the ground or under a deck where snow can accumulate. The intake should be at least 12 inches above grade and 3 feet from any dryer or bathroom exhaust vent. In areas with heavy snowfall, consider extending the intake above the roof line.

### Condensate Drain Line Freeze Protection

As mentioned, the condensate drain is a weak point. Best practices include:

1.  Running the drain line through conditioned space whenever possible
2.  Using 3/4-inch PVC instead of 1/2-inch to reduce clogging risk
3.  Installing a [condensate pump](https://hvaclaboratory.com/api/hutts-analytics/go?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.amazon.com%2Fs%3Fk%3Dhvac%2Bcondensate%2Bpump%26tag%3Dhvaclaboratory-20&n=amazon)
     with a high-temperature shutoff if the drain must go uphill
4.  Wrapping exposed drain lines with heat tape and insulation
5.  Adding a secondary drain line or overflow switch for safety

Some technicians install a condensate drain trap heater kit, which is a low-wattage heating element that keeps the trap from freezing. This is a worthwhile addition in climates where temperatures regularly drop below 0°F.

### Ductwork Sealing and Insulation

Ducts running through attics, crawlspaces, or garages lose significant heat in cold weather. In very cold climates, all ductwork in unconditioned spaces should be sealed with mastic (not tape) and insulated to at least R-8. Supply ducts close to the furnace should be insulated to prevent condensation on the exterior surface. Return ducts in cold spaces can pull in freezing air, causing the furnace to run longer and potentially freeze the condensate in the heat exchanger.

Troubleshooting Cold-Weather Furnace Failures
---------------------------------------------

When a furnace fails during a cold snap, the technician needs to diagnose quickly and accurately. Here is a systematic approach for very cold climates.

### Step 1: Check for Frozen Condensate

The most common cause of no-heat calls in extreme cold is a frozen condensate drain line. If the furnace is a condensing model and the pressure switch is open, check the drain line for ice. Look for water backup in the drain hose or trap. If the line is frozen, thaw it with a heat gun (carefully, avoiding PVC damage) or pour warm water through the drain port. Do not use boiling water, as it can crack PVC.

### Step 2: Verify Combustion Air and Venting

Check that the intake and exhaust vents are clear of snow, ice, and debris. In windy conditions, a pressure switch fault may be intermittent. Use a manometer to measure the pressure differential across the switch. If the switch is opening at the correct setpoint, the problem is likely venting or wind-related. Consider installing a wind-resistant vent cap or relocating the termination.

### Step 3: Measure Gas Pressure

Use a manometer to check manifold gas pressure at the furnace. For natural gas, this should typically be 3.5 inches WC for most furnaces. For propane, it is usually 10–11 inches WC. If the pressure is low, check the gas line size, regulator, and meter. In extreme cold, propane systems may need a larger tank or a vaporizer to maintain pressure.

### Step 4: Inspect the Heat Exchanger

Extreme temperature swings can cause heat exchanger cracks. Use a combustion analyzer to check for carbon monoxide in the airstream. A cracked heat exchanger in a very cold climate can be especially dangerous because the furnace runs longer, increasing the risk of CO exposure. If CO is detected, shut down the furnace immediately and recommend replacement.

When to Call a Senior Technician or Inspector
---------------------------------------------

Some cold-weather furnace issues go beyond routine troubleshooting and require a more experienced technician or a code inspector. Recognize these situations:

*   **Recurring pressure switch faults** after venting and drain checks—may indicate a heat exchanger restriction or improper vent sizing that requires engineering review.
*   **Gas supply problems** that persist after checking the meter and regulator—may involve the utility company or a propane supplier.
*   **Structural issues** like ice dams or frost accumulation on the roof that affect vent terminations—may require a building inspector or roofer.
*   **Carbon monoxide readings** above 9 ppm in the airstream—immediate shutdown and replacement required; document findings for liability.
*   **Furnace sizing disputes** where the homeowner insists the unit is undersized but the load calculation shows otherwise—a second opinion from a senior tech or a Manual J audit may be needed.

In very cold climates, the margin for error is small. A furnace that is 10% undersized may work fine in a mild winter but fail during a polar vortex. Senior technicians should be consulted for any installation that deviates from standard practice, such as venting through an unheated attic or using a non-condensing furnace in a climate where condensing is recommended.

Practical Takeaway for Technicians
----------------------------------

Gas furnace performance in very cold climates is not a mystery, but it demands attention to details that are often overlooked in moderate regions. The three pillars are proper sizing via Manual J, sealed combustion with freeze-protected condensate drains, and verification of gas supply under peak load. Every installation in a very cold climate should include a condensate drain freeze prevention plan, a combustion air intake located above the snow line, and ductwork sealed and insulated to R-8 or better. When in doubt, consult the manufacturer’s installation instructions for cold-weather addenda—many have specific requirements for temperatures below 0°F. A furnace that performs reliably at -20°F is the result of careful design, not luck.

How Heat Pumps Work (and Why Climate Matters)
---------------------------------------------

A heat pump does not generate heat, it moves heat from one place to another using a refrigeration cycle. In winter, it extracts heat from outdoor air (even cold air contains heat energy) and transfers it indoors. In summer, it reverses the process, working like an air conditioner by removing heat from your home.

This is fundamentally different from a gas furnace, which burns natural gas to create heat. Because a heat pump moves heat rather than generating it, it can deliver 2 to 4 units of heat for every 1 unit of electricity consumed. A gas furnace, by comparison, can only convert 80-96% of the gas energy into heat, it can never exceed 1:1 efficiency.

Climate matters because a heat pump's efficiency drops as outdoor temperatures fall. There is less heat energy available in colder air, so the system must work harder. Use our [Heat Pump Calculator](https://jouleio.com/heat-pump-calculator/)
 to estimate operating costs for your specific climate and electricity rates.

Efficiency by Temperature: COP Explained
----------------------------------------

COP (Coefficient of Performance) measures heat pump efficiency at a specific temperature. A COP of 3.0 means the heat pump produces 3 kWh of heat for every 1 kWh of electricity consumed. Here is how COP changes with outdoor temperature for different heat pump types.

| Outdoor Temp | Standard Heat Pump | Cold-Climate HP | Gas Furnace (equiv.) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 60°F (16°C) | COP 4.0 | COP 4.5 | COP 0.92 |
| 40°F (4°C) | COP 3.0 | COP 3.5 | COP 0.92 |
| 25°F (-4°C) | COP 2.0 | COP 2.8 | COP 0.92 |
| 10°F (-12°C) | COP 1.2 | COP 2.2 | COP 0.92 |
| \-5°F (-21°C) | Backup heat | COP 1.6 | COP 0.92 |

Even at 10°F, a cold-climate heat pump delivers 2.2 kWh of heat per 1 kWh of electricity, more than twice the efficiency of a gas furnace. The crossover point where a standard heat pump becomes less cost-effective than gas depends on your local electricity and gas prices. Check your rates with our [Electricity Cost Calculator](https://jouleio.com/electricity-cost-calculator/)
.

Warm Climates (Zones 8-10): Clear Heat Pump Winner
--------------------------------------------------

In warm climates like Miami, Houston, Phoenix, and the Gulf Coast, heat pumps are the obvious choice. Heating needs are minimal (500-1,500 heating hours per year), temperatures rarely drop below 40°F, and the heat pump doubles as your air conditioner for the dominant cooling season.

### Annual Operating Cost Comparison

| Cost Category | Heat Pump | Gas Furnace + AC |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Heating | $180 - $320 | $300 - $500 |
| Cooling | $600 - $1,100 | $650 - $1,200 |
| Total Annual | $780 - $1,420 | $950 - $1,700 |

**Verdict:** Heat pumps save $170-$280 per year in warm climates. They also eliminate the need for a separate AC unit, simplifying your HVAC system and reducing maintenance costs. This is a no-brainer region for heat pump adoption.

Mild Climates (Zones 6-7): Heat Pump Advantage
----------------------------------------------

Mild climate regions include cities like Charlotte, Nashville, Atlanta, Sacramento, and Portland. These areas experience moderate winters (2,000-3,500 heating hours) with temperatures typically staying above 20°F. Standard heat pumps perform well here without supplemental heating.

### Annual Operating Cost Comparison

| Cost Category | Heat Pump | Gas Furnace + AC |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Heating | $450 - $750 | $600 - $1,000 |
| Cooling | $350 - $650 | $400 - $700 |
| Total Annual | $800 - $1,400 | $1,000 - $1,700 |

In mild climates, heat pumps consistently save $200-$300 annually compared to gas furnace plus AC combinations. The average COP during heating season stays above 2.5, making electricity a more cost-effective fuel than natural gas in most of these markets. Pair a heat pump with solar for even greater savings, check our [Carbon Footprint Calculator](https://jouleio.com/carbon-footprint-calculator/)
 to see the environmental benefit.

Cold Climates (Zones 4-5): The Close Call
-----------------------------------------

Cold climate regions include Chicago, Denver, Boston, Philadelphia, and the upper Midwest. These areas have extended heating seasons (4,000-6,000 heating hours) with extended periods below 25°F. Standard heat pumps need supplemental electric resistance heat during the coldest stretches, which reduces their cost advantage.

### Standard Heat Pump vs Cold-Climate Heat Pump

| System | Heating Cost | Cooling Cost | Total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Standard Heat Pump | $1,100 - $1,600 | $250 - $450 | $1,350 - $2,050 |
| Cold-Climate Heat Pump | $750 - $1,200 | $250 - $450 | $1,000 - $1,650 |
| Gas Furnace + AC | $800 - $1,300 | $300 - $500 | $1,100 - $1,800 |

In cold climates, the comparison is closer. A standard heat pump may cost more to operate than a gas furnace during harsh winters due to backup electric resistance heat. However, a cold-climate heat pump with a variable-speed compressor avoids this penalty and typically matches or beats gas furnace costs, even in zones 4-5.

The critical variable is the ratio of electricity price to gas price. When electricity costs less than 3x the price of gas (per BTU equivalent), heat pumps win. In most U.S. markets, this threshold is met. Use our [Heat Pump Calculator](https://jouleio.com/heat-pump-calculator/)
 to compare costs with your actual utility rates.

Very Cold Climates (Zones 2-3): Cold-Climate Heat Pumps
-------------------------------------------------------

Very cold regions like Minneapolis, Anchorage, Fargo, and northern New England experience extreme winters with temperatures regularly below 0°F. Historically, heat pumps were impractical here. Modern cold-climate models have changed that calculus dramatically.

Cold-climate heat pumps (ccASHP) from manufacturers like Mitsubishi, Daikin, Fujitsu, and Bosch use variable-speed inverter compressors, enhanced vapor injection, and larger heat exchangers to maintain performance at extreme temperatures. The Mitsubishi Hyper-Heating line, for example, produces rated heating capacity down to -13°F.

Even in zone 2-3 climates, a cold-climate heat pump combined with modest backup heating (gas or electric) achieves annual operating costs comparable to a high-efficiency gas furnace. States like Maine and Vermont have aggressive heat pump rebate programs specifically because the economics work even in their harsh winters. Many homeowners keep their existing furnace as backup and use the heat pump for 80-90% of heating hours, achieving significant savings.

Installation Cost Comparison
----------------------------

Understanding upfront costs is essential for a complete economic comparison. Remember that a heat pump replaces both your furnace and air conditioner.

| System | Equipment | Installation | Total Installed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Standard Heat Pump | $2,500 - $5,000 | $1,500 - $3,000 | $4,000 - $8,000 |
| Cold-Climate Heat Pump | $4,000 - $8,000 | $2,000 - $4,000 | $6,000 - $12,000 |
| Gas Furnace | $1,500 - $4,000 | $1,500 - $3,000 | $3,000 - $7,000 |
| Gas Furnace + Central AC | $4,000 - $8,000 | $2,500 - $5,000 | $6,500 - $13,000 |

When comparing apples to apples, a heat pump versus a furnace plus AC, the installation costs are surprisingly similar. The heat pump provides both heating and cooling in a single system, while the furnace setup requires separate heating and cooling equipment. State and utility rebates for heat pumps can further tilt the equation in their favor (the federal 25C heat pump credit ended for systems placed in service after 2025).

15-Year Total Cost of Ownership
-------------------------------

The most meaningful comparison looks at total cost of ownership over the system's lifetime, including installation, operating costs, maintenance, and potential equipment replacement.

| Climate Zone | Heat Pump (15-yr) | Gas + AC (15-yr) | HP Savings |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Warm (8-10) | $22,000 | $28,500 | $6,500 |
| Mild (6-7) | $24,000 | $30,000 | $6,000 |
| Cold (4-5) | $28,500 | $31,000 | $2,500 |
| Very Cold (2-3) | $34,000 | $33,000 | \-$1,000\* |

\*In very cold climates, cold-climate heat pumps may cost slightly more over 15 years if gas prices are low. However, factoring in the Inflation Reduction Act's heat pump rebates ($2,000-$8,000 for qualifying households) and rising natural gas prices can close or eliminate the gap. The environmental benefit of electrified heating, especially with renewable electricity, is an additional consideration for many homeowners.

Frequently Asked Questions
--------------------------

### At what temperature do heat pumps become inefficient?

Standard air-source heat pumps lose efficiency below 40°F and struggle below 25°F. Cold-climate models maintain efficiency down to 5°F and continue operating at -15°F, though at reduced capacity.

### Are heat pumps cheaper to run than gas furnaces?

In warm and mild climates (zones 7-10), heat pumps consistently save $200-$600/year. In cold climates (zones 4-6), it depends on local electricity and gas prices. Use our [Heat Pump Calculator](https://jouleio.com/heat-pump-calculator/)
 with your rates.

### How much does a heat pump cost to install vs a gas furnace?

A standard heat pump costs $4,000-$8,000 installed; a cold-climate model runs $6,000-$12,000. A gas furnace costs $3,000-$7,000. But heat pumps provide both heating and cooling, potentially eliminating a separate $3,000-$5,000 AC unit.

### Do heat pumps work in cold climates like Minnesota or Maine?

Yes. Modern cold-climate heat pumps from Mitsubishi, Daikin, and Bosch heat homes efficiently down to -13°F. Maine has over 100,000 heat pumps installed, one of the highest adoption rates in the U.S.

### What is COP and HSPF and why do they matter?

COP (Coefficient of Performance) measures heat output per unit of electricity at a specific temperature. HSPF (Heating Seasonal Performance Factor) is the seasonal average. Higher values mean lower operating costs. A gas furnace has an effective COP of 0.80-0.96, while heat pumps typically achieve 2.0-4.5 depending on conditions.

Calculate Your Heat Pump Savings
--------------------------------

Compare heat pump vs furnace costs for your specific climate and energy rates.

In addition, supplemental information provided by manufacturers to demonstrate performance in cold temperatures is not standardized or consistent. The current performance metric (HSPF) does not include low temperature testing points below 17°F, assumes the use of electric resistance elements, and tests in steady-state operation (as opposed to allowing modulation). These deficiencies add up to measurements that do not accurately reflect performance of the latest generation of air source heat pumps. In order to address stakeholder concerns about these deficiencies, a group of interested stakeholders - working together as part of the [Heating Electrification Initiative](https://neep.org/ashp) (facilitated by NEEP) - developed the specification to better characterize heat pump performance ([now on V](https://neep.org/sites/default/files/media-files/cold_climate_air-source_heat_pump_specification-version_3.1_update_.pdf) [4.0](https://neep.org/sites/default/files/media-files/cold_climate_air_source_heat_pump_specification_-_version_4.0_final_1.pdf) ). Initiative participants include energy efficiency program administrators, heat pump installers, state energy office staff, and technology experts.  The specification was designed to identify air source heat pumps that are best suited to heat efficiently in cold climates (IECC climate zone 4 and higher). It is intended as a model equipment specification to be used broadly by clean energy and energy efficiency program administrators in cold climates as a minimum requirement for program qualification. It is also intended for engineers, contractors, and other practitioners who need assurance that the equipment they select will have the required heating capacity at design temperature without unnecessary oversizing, and will serve the load efficiently throughout the ambient temperature range. More details on the process taken to arrive at the V3.0 specification are in the [V3.0 Specification Memo](https://neep.org/sites/default/files/ColdClimateAirSourceHeatPumpSpecification-Version3.0FINALMEMO.pdf) . In 2021, NEEP worked with its network of stakeholders and NYSERDA to develop a packaged terminal heat pump (PTHP) specification. Research and feedback led to the addition of single package vertical heat pumps (SPVHPs). Both small form-factor products have recently become available with variable speed compressors, allowing operation at 5°F and below without supplementary electric heat. As architects, engineers, and energy efficiency program administrators look for options to replace aging packaged terminal air conditioners (PTACs) common in high-rise multi-family homes, particularly in cities like New York, the NEEP list will identify products best suited to electrify heating in cold climates. In cooperation with regional and national stakeholders including federal agencies, program administrators, and manufacturers, NEEP launched ccASHP Version 4.0. in 2022. Effective January 1st, 2023, the ccASHP Specification encompasses all previous heat pump categories, including the long standing HP category, recently added Packaged Terminal Heat Pump (PTHP) and Single Package Vertical Heat Pump (SPVHP) categories, and a new Variable Refrigerant Flow (VRF) Multi-Split Heat Pump category. Covering the foundation of cold climate air source heat pumps currently available on the market, the NEEP ccASHP Product List and Specification provide a resource to programs, manufacturers, contractors, and consumers to drive adoption of heat pumps in cold climates. For Manufacturers ----------------- **Why List Products?** Listing products on the NEEP ccASHP Product List makes standardized cold-climate performance data available to contractors, designers, consumers, utilities, and program administrators through a widely used industry resource. Listing can increase product visibility, help users compare and select systems, and make it easier for programs that reference the Product List to identify products for potential incentive eligibility.   By participating, manufacturers also support a more transparent and consistent market for high-performing ccASHPs.
