findings.title: www.hvacbase.org
findings.query: cold climate heat pump performance low temperature
findings.content:
Yes — modern cold-climate heat pumps work effectively down to −15 °F and some models operate as low as −22 °F. A 2026-era cold-climate heat pump maintains 75–100% of its rated heating capacity at 5 °F and still delivers heat at COP 1.5–2.0 well below zero, which is 50–100% more efficient than electric resistance backup.

The old conventional wisdom that heat pumps "stop working below freezing" is based on 1980s-era technology. Today's inverter-driven, vapor-injection compressors have fundamentally changed the equation. Norway, Finland, and Sweden — where winter temps regularly hit −10 °F to −30 °F — lead the world in heat pump adoption. This guide shows you exactly how cold-weather performance works, using manufacturer spec sheets and DOE / NEEP cold-climate program data.

How Cold Is Too Cold?
---------------------

There's no single "too cold" temperature — it depends on your specific heat pump model. Here's the operating range by category.

| Category | Full Capacity Down To | Reduced Capacity Down To | Shuts Off Below | Typical COP at 5 °F |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Standard heat pump | 30–40 °F | 5–15 °F | 0–10 °F | 1.3–1.8 |
| Cold-climate rated | 5–15 °F | −13 to −5 °F | −15 to −5 °F | 1.8–3.0 |
| Extreme cold-climate | 5 °F | −22 to −15 °F | −22 °F | 2.0–3.2 |
| Ground-source (geothermal) | Any (ground is 45–65 °F) | Any | N/A | 3.5–4.5 |

The key distinction: a "cold-climate" heat pump (as defined by NEEP and the DOE) must maintain at least 70% of its rated capacity at 5 °F and operate down to −15 °F or below. Standard heat pumps don't meet this threshold and lose capacity rapidly below 25 °F. To size cold-climate capacity against your specific design temperature, use the [heat pump size calculator](https://www.hvacbase.org/heat-pump-size-calculator)
; for the geothermal alternative (which maintains COP 3.5–4.5 regardless of outdoor temperature), see the [air-source vs ground-source comparison](https://www.hvacbase.org/air-source-vs-ground-source-heat-pump)
.

Warning

**Critical for Northern Homeowners:** If you live in IECC climate zones 5–7, do NOT install a standard heat pump as your primary heat source. The capacity loss below 15 °F means heavy reliance on expensive backup heat. Invest in a model specifically rated for cold-climate operation — the upfront premium of $1,000–$3,000 pays for itself in one to two heating seasons.

Performance Data by Temperature
-------------------------------

This is the most important table in this article. It shows how three representative heat pump categories perform across a range of outdoor temperatures.

| Outdoor Temp | Standard HP Capacity | Standard HP COP | Cold-Climate HP Capacity | Cold-Climate COP | Electricity Cost/Hour\* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 47 °F | 36,000 BTU (100%) | 3.8 | 36,000 BTU (100%) | 4.2 | $0.35–$0.40 |
| 35 °F | 30,000 BTU (83%) | 3.2 | 34,000 BTU (94%) | 3.6 | $0.38–$0.44 |
| 25 °F | 24,000 BTU (67%) | 2.6 | 32,000 BTU (89%) | 3.1 | $0.42–$0.52 |
| 17 °F | 20,000 BTU (56%) | 2.1 | 30,000 BTU (83%) | 2.7 | $0.46–$0.58 |
| 5 °F | 14,000 BTU (39%) | 1.6 | 28,000 BTU (78%) | 2.3 | $0.52–$0.68 |
| 0 °F | 10,000 BTU (28%) | 1.3 | 26,000 BTU (72%) | 2.0 | $0.58–$0.78 |
| \-5 °F | Shuts off or \`<8\`K BTU | 1.0–1.2 | 24,000 BTU (67%) | 1.8 | $0.62–$0.82 |
| \-13 °F | Off | —   | 20,000 BTU (56%) | 1.5 | $0.68–$0.92 |
| \-22 °F | Off | —   | 14,000 BTU (39%)\*\* | 1.2 | $0.78–$1.02 |

\*Cost assumes 3-ton unit, $0.18/kWh (illustrative). \*\*Only select extreme-cold models reach −22 °F; verify the specific model's minimum heating operating temperature on the manufacturer spec sheet. The Fujitsu XLTH is rated to −15 °F per the Fujitsu General spec sheet.

The takeaway: a cold-climate heat pump at 0 °F delivers roughly the same capacity and efficiency that a standard heat pump achieves at 35 °F. It shifts the entire performance curve downward by approximately 30–35 degrees.

Why Modern Heat Pumps Handle Cold Better
----------------------------------------

Three technologies have transformed cold-weather heat pump performance since the 2010s.

### 1\. Inverter-Driven Variable-Speed Compressors

Older heat pumps used fixed-speed compressors that ran at 100% or 0%. Modern inverter compressors modulate their speed continuously from about 20% to 120% of rated capacity. In cold weather, the inverter can overclock the compressor to produce more heat than the system's rated capacity, compensating for the lower COP.

This "boost" mode is why some cold-climate units actually deliver more than 100% rated capacity at moderate cold temperatures (15–35 °F) — the compressor spins faster to extract more heat from the cold air.

### 2\. Enhanced Vapor Injection (EVI)

EVI technology adds a secondary heat exchanger that pre-heats the refrigerant before it enters the compressor. This raises the compressor's discharge temperature, allowing it to deliver warmer supply air even when outdoor temperatures are very low. EVI is the key technology behind brands like Mitsubishi Hyper-Heat, Fujitsu XLTH, and Daikin Aurora.

Without EVI, refrigerant returning to the compressor from very cold outdoor air is so cold that the compressor can't raise it to a useful temperature. With EVI, the system maintains supply air temperatures of 100–110 °F even when it's −10 °F outside.

### 3\. Advanced Refrigerants

The transition from R-22 (older systems) to R-410A and now R-32 has improved low-temperature performance. R-32 has a wider operating temperature range and better thermodynamic properties at low ambient temperatures than R-410A, which is one reason why the newest cold-climate models (most of which use R-32) outperform their predecessors.

Good to Know

**The Scandinavian Proof of Concept:** Norway installed its first air-source heat pump in 1973. By 2026, over 60% of Norwegian homes use heat pumps as their primary heat source — in a country where winter temperatures routinely hit −10 °F to −20 °F. Finland and Sweden aren't far behind. The technology is proven in climates far colder than most of the continental U.S.

Cold Climate vs Standard Heat Pumps
-----------------------------------

| Feature | Standard Heat Pump | Cold-Climate Heat Pump |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Compressor type | Fixed or basic inverter | Advanced inverter with EVI |
| Minimum operating temp | 0 to 10 °F | −13 to −22 °F |
| Capacity at 5 °F | 30–45% of rated | 75–100% of rated |
| COP at 5 °F | 1.3–1.8 | 2.0–3.0 |
| Base pan heater | Sometimes | Always included |
| Defrost system | Timed (basic) | Demand-based (intelligent) |
| Supply air temp at 0 °F | 85–95 °F | 100–110 °F |
| Refrigerant | R-410A | R-32 (most new models) |
| HSPF2 | 8.0–9.5 | 10.0–14.2 |
| Installed cost (3-ton) | $5,800–$9,000 | $8,000–$13,000 |
| Cost premium | —   | +$2,000–$4,000 |
| Best for zones | 1–4 | 4–7 |

For a full installed-cost breakdown by system type, size, and region, see our [heat pump installation cost guide](https://www.hvacbase.org/heat-pump-cost-to-install/)
. For the winter-vs-summer kWh split in cold climates, see our [heat pump electricity usage guide](https://www.hvacbase.org/heat-pump-electricity-usage/)
.

The Defrost Problem (And How It's Solved)
-----------------------------------------

When outdoor temperatures are between 25 °F and 40 °F with high humidity, frost builds up on the outdoor heat exchanger coil. The heat pump must periodically reverse its cycle to melt this frost — a process called defrost. During defrost, the system briefly sends warm refrigerant to the outdoor coil (melting the ice) while the indoor unit stops heating. If backup strip heat is installed, it may activate to prevent cold air from blowing into the home.

### How Defrost Affects Performance

Each defrost cycle lasts 5–15 minutes and temporarily reduces heating output. In the worst conditions (30–40 °F with fog or drizzle), defrost may occur 2–4 times per hour, reducing the system's effective heating capacity by 10–15% during that period.

**Why cold-climate models defrost better:** They use "demand defrost" with sensors that measure actual coil temperature and ice buildup, rather than simple timers. This means the system only defrosts when truly needed, reducing unnecessary cycles by 30–50%. Many cold-climate models also have base pan heaters that keep the outdoor unit's drain pan clear of ice, preventing water from refreezing and blocking airflow.

**Counter-intuitive fact:** Defrost issues are actually worse at 30–40 °F than at 0 °F. Very cold air holds little moisture, so frost buildup is minimal at extreme low temperatures. The worst defrost conditions are humid, near-freezing weather — common in the Pacific Northwest, Mid-Atlantic, and parts of the Midwest.

Backup Heat Strategies
----------------------

Even the best cold-climate heat pump may benefit from a backup heat strategy. Here are the four main approaches, ranked by cost-effectiveness.

| Strategy | How It Works | Installed Cost | Operating Cost | Best For |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| No backup (cold-climate HP sized to load) | HP handles 100% of heating | $0 additional | Lowest | Zones 4–6, well-insulated homes |
| Dual-fuel / hybrid (HP + gas furnace) | HP heats above 25–35°F; furnace below | $0 if keeping existing furnace | Low–moderate | Zones 5–7, homes with existing gas |
| Electric resistance strips | 5–15 kW strips in air handler | $200–$600 | High when active | Zones 4–5, infrequent use only |
| Wood / pellet stove | Manual backup for extreme events | $1,500–$4,000 | Low (fuel cost) | Rural homes, power outage backup |

### Option 1: No Backup (Cold-Climate HP Sized to Load)

The cleanest approach: size a cold-climate heat pump to meet your home's full heating load at the design temperature (the coldest temp expected 99% of winter hours). For a well-insulated 2,000 sq ft home in Minneapolis (design temp −12 °F), this might mean a 3.5–4 ton Mitsubishi or Fujitsu system.

This works when: your home is well-insulated, the heat pump is properly sized to the actual heating load (not guessed), and you accept that during the 10–20 coldest hours of the year, the system may run continuously at maximum capacity.

### Option 2: Dual-Fuel / Hybrid

The most popular approach in cold climates. You keep your existing gas furnace and add a heat pump. A thermostat-controlled switchover point (typically 25–35 °F) tells the system to use the heat pump above that temperature and the furnace below it.

This captures heat pump efficiency for 70–85% of heating hours while using gas only during the coldest periods. It's especially cost-effective if your furnace is less than 10 years old and still in good condition.

### Option 3: Electric Resistance Strips

The cheapest to install but most expensive to operate. Strip heaters (5–15 kW) in the air handler activate when the heat pump can't keep up. At ~$0.18/kWh, a 10 kW strip costs ≈$1.80/hour — versus ≈$0.50–$0.90/hour for the heat pump (illustrative). Use only if backup activates fewer than 100 hours per winter.

### Option 4: Supplemental Wood/Pellet Stove

A wood stove in the main living area provides radiant heat that doesn't depend on electricity or the HVAC system. It's a robust backup for power outages and can significantly offset heating costs during the coldest periods. The main drawback is that heat doesn't distribute evenly to other rooms without ductwork or fans.

Sizing for Cold Climates
------------------------

Proper sizing is even more critical in cold climates than in moderate ones. You need to size based on the heating load at your local design temperature, not the cooling load.

**Step 1: Get a Manual J load calculation.** This determines your home's actual heating requirement in BTU/h at the design temperature.

**Step 2: Match the heat pump's capacity at design temperature.** A 3-ton (36K BTU) heat pump that maintains 78% capacity at 5 °F delivers 28,080 BTU at that temperature. If your design-temp load is 35,000 BTU, you need the next size up.

**Step 3: Verify the system's balance point.** The balance point is the outdoor temperature where the heat pump's capacity exactly matches the home's heating load. Below the balance point, supplemental heat is needed. A well-sized cold-climate system has a balance point at or below your design temperature, meaning no backup is needed.

| Sizing Approach | System Size | Capacity at −12 °F | Meets 42K BTU Load? | Backup Needed? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Undersized (common mistake) | 3 ton (36K rated) | 18,000 BTU (50%) | No — 24K BTU gap | Yes, heavy use |
| Properly sized (standard) | 4 ton (48K rated) | 28,800 BTU (60%) | No — 13K BTU gap | Yes, moderate use |
| Properly sized (cold-climate) | 3.5 ton cold-climate (42K rated) | 33,600 BTU (80%) | Close — 8K gap | Yes, light use |
| Oversized cold-climate | 4 ton cold-climate (48K rated) | 38,400 BTU (80%) | Close — 4K gap | Minimal |
| Right-sized + envelope upgrades | 3 ton cold-climate + insulation | 28,800 BTU / 30K load | Yes (load reduced) | No  |

Pro Tip

**The Smart Approach:** Before buying a bigger heat pump, invest in reducing your heating load. Adding attic insulation from R-30 to R-60 ($1,500–$3,000) and air sealing ($500–$1,500) can reduce your heating load by 20–30%. That might drop your 42K BTU load to 30K BTU, allowing a smaller, less expensive heat pump to handle the job without backup.

Cold-Climate Installation Details
---------------------------------

Cold-climate operation places extra demands on the outdoor unit and refrigerant lines. Four install details make a meaningful difference in reliability and efficiency once the outdoor temperature drops below freezing.

**Insulate the line set thickly.** Refrigerant lines should carry closed-cell insulation of at least 3/4-inch thickness. Poorly-insulated suction lines lose meaningful heat to the ambient cold, reducing system efficiency during the coldest hours.

**Install a wind barrier if the unit faces prevailing winter winds.** A fence panel or dense shrub row placed 3–4 feet from the outdoor unit reduces the effective coldness on the coil and preserves heating capacity. Do not enclose the unit — it needs unrestricted airflow on all sides.

**Manage defrost drainage.** Condensate from the defrost cycle must drain clear of the outdoor unit. In freezing weather, poorly-drained condensate forms ice dams that can damage the unit or shorten its life. Use a heated drain line, or slope the drain area so meltwater flows well away from the unit and keep the area clear of debris and snow through the winter.

**Verify the pan heater on the spec sheet.** Most cold-climate units ship with a base-pan heater that prevents ice accumulation in the drain pan during defrost cycles. Confirm this on the spec sheet before purchasing — it is often the difference between a unit that works in Zone 6 and one that ices up by February.

### Additional cold-climate model references

Beyond the Fujitsu XLTH and Mitsubishi Hyper-Heat models discussed above, several other units carry cold-climate specifications worth verifying at the [AHRI Directory](https://www.ahridirectory.org/)
:

*   **Senville LETO SENL-12CD** — rated to −13 °F per the manufacturer spec sheet.
*   **Cooper & Hunter HPR line** — manufacturer-rated to approximately −22 °F for select configurations (not AHRI-certified — manufacturer-rated only).
*   **LG Art Cool Premier** — rated continuous down to −13 °F (R-410A models; production has stopped, so verify current availability before quoting).

For any specific match, confirm the AHRI Certified Reference Number (status: Active), the low-temperature heating capacity, and refrigerant type before purchase. AHRI-certified numbers are the only ones covered by manufacturer warranty language.

### State and utility rebates for cold-climate installs

Several Northeastern and Pacific-Northwest states run cold-climate heat pump rebate programs that meaningfully offset install cost — Mass Save (Massachusetts), Efficiency Maine, NYSERDA Clean Heat (New York), Efficiency Vermont, and PSE / Seattle City Light are examples. Rebate amounts and eligibility change frequently and vary by ZIP code, so we do not list specific dollar figures here; check the [DSIRE database](https://www.dsireusa.org/)
 or contact your state energy office for current amounts.

The federal Section 25C tax credit is no longer available for 2026 installs (terminated Dec 31, 2025 under OBBBA), but the IRA-funded HEAR (income-qualified, up to $8,000 point-of-sale) and HOMES (open to all incomes, performance-based) rebate programs survived and remain the active federal pathway.

Key Takeaways
-------------

Key Takeaway

Modern cold-climate heat pumps work effectively down to **−15 °F** (some to −22 °F), maintaining COP 1.5–2.0 even well below zero. At 5 °F, cold-climate models retain **75–100% of rated capacity** versus 30–45% for standard models. The key technologies are **inverter compressors, enhanced vapor injection (EVI), and R-32 refrigerant**. Defrost issues are worst at 30–40 °F, not at extreme cold temperatures. **Dual-fuel (hybrid) systems** offer the best of both worlds in zones 6–7. Proper sizing to the **heating design load at design temperature** is critical. Norway, Finland, and Sweden prove heat pumps work in the coldest inhabited climates on Earth.

Frequently Asked Questions
--------------------------

Why does my heat pump blow cold air in winter?

Common causes include normal defrost mode (5–15 minutes, system temporarily reverses), the thermostat set to "fan on" instead of "auto," outdoor temperature below the unit's minimum operating threshold, low refrigerant charge, or a stuck reversing valve. If cold air persists beyond a defrost cycle, contact a technician. Do not switch to "emergency heat" unless the heat pump is actually broken.

How do heat pumps work in Scandinavian winters?

How Heat Pumps Work And Why Temperature Matters
-----------------------------------------------

Heat pumps move heat from one place to another using refrigerant and a compressor rather than generating heat by combustion or resistance. Air-source units extract heat from outdoor air; ground-source units extract heat from the earth. **Temperature matters** because the amount of heat available in the source (air or ground) determines how hard the compressor must work and how efficiently the system operates.

Minimum Operating Temperature Versus Practical Heating Limit
------------------------------------------------------------

There are two distinct concepts: the **minimum operating temperature** at which a heat pump continues to function and the **practical heating limit** where it can supply enough heat to meet a home’s load without backup. Manufacturers often list lower operating limits, but heating capacity declines as outdoor temperature drops.

Air-Source Heat Pumps: Typical Limits And Performance
-----------------------------------------------------

Traditional air-source heat pumps historically lost efficiency below about 25°F (-4°C). Modern units, especially those labeled “cold-climate,” are designed to operate down to 0°F (-18°C) and continue producing usable heat even lower, though with reduced capacity.

Key performance metric is **COP (Coefficient Of Performance)**, the ratio of heat output to electrical energy input. COP falls with outdoor temperature; a unit with COP 3 at 47°F might drop to COP 1.5 at 5°F, meaning greater electricity use per unit of heat.

Cold-Climate Air-Source And Mini-Split Models
---------------------------------------------

Manufacturers now produce cold-climate air-source and ductless mini-split heat pumps rated for very low temperatures. Some models can operate reliably at -13°F to -22°F (-25°C to -30°C) thanks to improved compressors, refrigerants, and controls. **Heat capacity** declines but often remains enough to heat well-insulated homes without fossil fuel backup in many climates.

Ground-Source (Geothermal) Heat Pumps: Stable Performance
---------------------------------------------------------

Ground-source heat pumps extract heat from the earth or groundwater, which maintains a relatively constant temperature below the frost line, typically 45°F–60°F (7°C–16°C) depending on location. This stability gives geothermal systems a consistent COP regardless of air temperature, effectively eliminating an air-temperature-based minimum operating limit.

Factors That Affect Minimum Practical Temperature
-------------------------------------------------

Several factors determine whether a heat pump can meet heating needs at low temperatures: system size, building envelope (insulation and air sealing), existing heating load, thermostat settings, and the presence of supplemental heat. **A properly sized system plus tight building envelope extends useful operating range.**

Defrost Cycles And Cold Weather Operation
-----------------------------------------

In cold, humid weather, outdoor coils can accumulate frost. Heat pumps periodically reverse operation to defrost the coil, temporarily reducing heating output. Modern systems use smart defrost controls to minimize energy loss; however, frequent defrosting can affect comfort and apparent capacity during cold snaps.

Backup Heat Options And Hybrid Strategies
-----------------------------------------

Because capacity drops as temperatures fall, many homeowners pair a heat pump with backup heat: electric resistance strips, gas furnace (dual-fuel), or hydronic auxiliary systems. **Hybrid systems** switch to backup when heat pump efficiency or capacity becomes insufficient, balancing comfort and cost.

Installation And Sizing Considerations For Cold Climates
--------------------------------------------------------

Proper design is critical. Oversizing can cause short cycling and reduced efficiency; undersizing leaves insufficient capacity on the coldest days. Heat load calculations (Manual J) should reflect worst-case temperatures. For cold climates, installers may specify a larger outdoor unit or a dual-fuel configuration to ensure reliable heating.

Tips To Improve Heat Pump Cold Weather Performance
--------------------------------------------------

*   **Upgrade Insulation And Air Sealing:** Reduce the heating load so the heat pump can meet demand at lower temperatures.
*   **Choose Cold-Climate Rated Units:** Look for models with low ambient performance ratings and high HSPF/SEER values.
*   **Consider Geothermal If Practical:** Higher upfront cost but consistent performance and lower operating cost in extreme cold.
*   **Install Smart Thermostats And Controls:** Optimize defrost cycles and prioritize comfort vs. efficiency.
*   **Provide A Backup Heat Source:** Use dual-fuel or electric backup sized for the building’s peak load.

Energy Efficiency Metrics And Ratings To Watch
----------------------------------------------

When comparing units, check the following metrics: **HSPF (Heating Seasonal Performance Factor)**, COP at specified temperatures, and cold-climate performance ratings such as rated capacity at 5°F (-15°C) or -4°F (-20°C). Higher HSPF and better low-ambient capacity indicate superior cold-weather performance.

Call [888-896-7031](tel:8779591215)
 for Free Local HVAC Quotes – Compare and Save Today!

Cost Considerations And Long-Term Savings
-----------------------------------------

Heat pump efficiency changes energy costs. Cold-climate models cost more upfront but yield greater savings in winter compared to lower-performing units. Ground-source systems have higher installation costs but deliver predictable, lower operating costs over time. Incentives, tax credits, and utility rebates can improve economics.

Common Myths And Realities
--------------------------

Myth: Heat pumps stop working below freezing. Reality: Most modern heat pumps continue to operate below freezing; performance decreases but often remains usable. Myth: Heat pumps are only for mild climates. Reality: Cold-climate and geothermal systems are designed for harsh winters and can replace or significantly reduce fossil fuel heating in many U.S. regions.

Maintenance And Long-Term Reliability In Cold Climates
------------------------------------------------------

Regular maintenance improves reliability: clean filters, inspect coils, ensure defrost controls work, and check refrigerant charge. Outdoor unit placement matters: elevated pads reduce snow burial risk and minimize ice buildup. Annual professional inspections catch issues early and maintain rated performance.

Choosing The Right System For Different U.S. Regions
----------------------------------------------------

In southern and mild northern states, standard air-source heat pumps often suffice. In cold northern regions, recommended strategies include cold-climate heat pumps, ductless mini-splits with low-ambient ratings, dual-fuel systems, or geothermal installations depending on budget and site constraints. Assess local climate data and heating degree days when planning.

Frequently Asked Questions
--------------------------

### What Is A Practical Minimum Temperature For Heat Pumps?

Practical minimum depends on the system: many modern air-source units can supply heat down to 0°F, cold-climate models to -13°F or lower, and geothermal systems remain effective regardless of air temperature. The home’s insulation and supplemental heat determine whether the heat pump alone can meet demand.

### Do Heat Pumps Require Backup In Very Cold Areas?

Often yes. Backup heat helps during extreme cold or when a heat pump’s capacity is insufficient. Dual-fuel systems that use gas or electric resistance backup are common solutions to maintain comfort while maximizing efficiency most of the time.

### How Does Defrost Affect Heating Capacity?

Defrost cycles temporarily reverse the system to melt frost, reducing heating output during the cycle. Smart defrost algorithms aim to minimize frequency and duration, but frequent frosting conditions can still impair effective heating during cold, wet periods.

### Are There Incentives For Cold-Climate Or Geothermal Heat Pumps?

Yes. Federal tax credits, state incentives, and utility rebates often apply to high-efficiency and geothermal heat pump installations. Eligibility varies; check current federal and local programs before purchase.

Resources And Further Reading
-----------------------------

Consult manufacturer specifications for low-ambient ratings and COP curves, read industry guidance such as the Air-Conditioning, Heating, and Refrigeration Institute (AHRI) performance data, and review federal and state energy program pages for incentives. Professional HVAC contractors should perform Manual J and system design for accurate sizing and selection.

**Final Practical Point:** Rather than focusing on a single minimum temperature, homeowners should evaluate heat pump performance across expected winter temperature ranges, building heat load, and the availability of backup systems. With appropriate design and modern cold-climate equipment, heat pumps can provide efficient heating in most U.S. climates.

![](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%200%200'%3E%3C/svg%3E "a-New-Furnace")

In boxes 1-3, simply type in the numbers or use the Up/Down arrows to enter the right value.

Enter the gas furnace size you currently have or has been recommended to you by your HVAC contractor. The calculator works for furnaces up to 90,000 BTUs.

What about efficiency? It doesn’t matter for our purposes because we use input BTUs vs output BTUs.

But you need to understand the difference in order to get the most precise answer to your gas furnace vs heat pump question. The input BTUs is how much fuel the furnace burns. Output is how much heat from the burn chamber gets transferred into your ductwork and home.

Using the example of an 60,000 BTU furnace and various efficiencies:

60K input x 80% efficiency = 48,000 BTUs of output

60K input x 90% efficiency = 54,000 BTUs of output

60K input x 95% efficiency = 57,000 BTUs of output

Output is the key number. So, determine what efficiency level is right for your home. The colder your climate, the more efficient the furnace should be. Let’s say you need 55,000 BTUs to adequately heat your home.

A 60,000 BTU furnace that is 95% efficient will do the job, delivering 57,000 BTUs.

But if you choose an 80% furnace because you live in a warmer climate, then you’ll have to jump to at least a 70,000 BTU furnace to get 56,000 BTUs.

**By the way,** if you don’t have a contractor, it makes sense to hire one to do a load calculation to find out exactly what size gas furnace or heat pump you need for your home. Getting sizing right is the only way to ensure your home will be adequately heated without overdoing it and wasting energy costs.

[Find Trusted HVAC Contractors & Get Free Quotes (pickhvac.com)](https://www.pickhvac.com/faq/free-estimate/)

### Box 2: Heat Pump Size by Ton

![maytag heat pump](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%200%200'%3E%3C/svg%3E "maytag heat pump")

Now enter the heat pump size. It typically won’t be the same as the gas furnace size. Options for residential heat pumps range from 1.5 to 5.0 tons, or 18,000 to 60,000 BTUs. Remember that heat pumps provide AC too, so if you live in a warm climate, you might need a large heat pump, even if you don’t require much heat.

### Box 3: Heat Pump HSPF Efficiency Rating

![what is hspf](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20360%20485'%3E%3C/svg%3E "hspf")

HSPF, or heating seasonal performance factor, is the heat pump efficiency. Today’s split system heat pumps range in efficiency from about 8.0 to 13.0 with 9.0 to 10.0 being the most common and cost-effective.

Guessing isn’t recommended. It’s always best to

### Box 4: Your State

The first option is the United States, but since costs vary so much from state to state, you’ll get more precise results by scrolling down and selecting where you live.

**“My state has a red background!”** That’s an indication that a heat pump isn’t the best fit for your climate. Heat pumps are very efficient and effective in climates ranging from hot to chilly. In cold climates of the North, they lose efficiency and often must rely on auxiliary heat strips that use electric resistance heat and are expensive to operate, raising your operating costs well above what you would pay to run a gas furnace.

### Box 5: Yearly Heating Hours

### Boxes 6 & 7: Electric Rates and Natural Gas Prices

### Results Box

The first line gives Yearly Total Savings.

Look at lines 2 & 3 to know whether it is cheaper to run a gas furnace or heat pump given the data you’ve inputted into the heat pump vs gas furnace running cost calculator.

From there, your savings are multiplied over 5, 10 and 15 years, which is about the standard lifespan for HVAC equipment (though many units last 20+ years).

Best Practices – Getting the Most Accurate Information
------------------------------------------------------

It is recommended that you have a licensed HVAC contractor/technician do a load calculation on your home to determine what size equipment you need.

Factors in a load calculation are your home size, insulation level, quality of the windows and doors, your climate and other lesser factors.

Additionally, the contractor can give you accurate sizes for the furnace and heat pump you’d need, so you can use this calculator to compare “apples to apples.”

It’s unlikely, as we noted, that if you need a 60,000 BTU furnace, a 60,000 BTU heat pump would be right for your home. For example, a home in a very warm state will need a relatively small furnace, maybe a 40,000 BTU unit. But because a heat pump also provides air conditioning, the heat pump might have to be 48,000 or 60,000 BTU.

### ****Sample 1: Warm Climate****

Let’s compare running costs in Georgia for a 40,000 BTU furnace vs a 48,000 BTU (4 ton) heat pump. The heat pump is bigger because it also has to cool the house in a hot, humid Georgia summer! When we use the calculator, here are the results:

**Gas Furnace Annual Running Cost: $1192**

**Heat Pump Annual Running Cost, 10.0 HSPF: $849**

In this example, you’ll save $344 per year using a 10 HSPF heat pump vs a gas furnace.

In 15 years, your savings would grow to more than $5K!

And the example compares an 80,000 BTU gas furnace with a 60,000 BTU or 5-ton heat pump. Chicago, by the way, is about as far north as we recommend using a heat pump vs a gas furnace. Since sizing your home’s HVAC equipment is vital, it makes sense to ask a pro to do the load calculation.

Understanding Cold Climate Heating Challenges --------------------------------------------- Cold climate heating involves more than just buying a powerful furnace. When outdoor temperatures drop below 0°F, your heating system faces challenges that milder climates never experience. Temperature differential between indoor and outdoor air increases significantly during extreme cold. A 70°F indoor temperature with -10°F outside creates an 80-degree differential that your furnace must continuously overcome. Heat loss accelerates in extreme conditions. Poor insulation, air leaks, and single-pane windows become major liabilities when the mercury plummets. Your furnace must work harder and longer to maintain comfortable temperatures. Short-cycling becomes a significant risk with oversized furnaces in cold climates. When a furnace is too large for the heating load, it heats the space quickly then shuts off, creating inefficient operation and uncomfortable temperature swings. **Expert Insight:** I’ve seen homeowners oversize their furnaces “to be safe” during extreme cold. This approach backfires, causing inefficiency, discomfort, and premature equipment failure. Proper sizing matters more than maximum capacity. Gas Furnace Buying Guide for Cold Climates ------------------------------------------ ### AFUE Rating Explained: What You Need for Cold Weather AFUE (Annual Fuel Utilization Efficiency) measures how much heat a furnace delivers compared to the fuel it consumes. A 97% AFUE furnace converts 97% of fuel energy into heat, wasting only 3%. For cold climates, I recommend minimum 96% AFUE efficiency. The Department of Energy now requires 92% AFUE minimum for northern states, but extreme cold justifies the extra investment in 96-97% models. The payback period for upgrading from 80% to 96% efficiency in cold climates typically ranges from 5-8 years. After that, you’re saving money every year compared to lower efficiency options. ### Single-Stage vs Two-Stage vs Modulating Furnaces Single-stage furnaces operate at full capacity or off. They’re simple and reliable but create temperature swings and less consistent comfort. Best for milder climates or budget-conscious installations. Two-stage furnaces operate at low fire (about 65% capacity) and high fire (100%). This provides much better comfort by matching output to conditions. I recommend two-stage for most cold climate installations as the best value. Modulating furnaces adjust output in 1-5% increments across their entire range. They provide the best comfort and efficiency but cost more upfront. This calculation considers your home’s square footage, insulation, windows, orientation, and local climate data. As a rough guide, homes in cold climates typically need 35-45 BTU per square foot. A 2,000 sq ft home might require 70,000-90,000 BTU capacity depending on construction quality and insulation. **Warning:** Never size your furnace based on the existing unit’s capacity. Previous owners may have installed incorrectly sized equipment. Always require a professional Manual J calculation. Heat Pumps vs. Gas Furnaces: 2026 Decision Guide
================================================

For most U.S. households, replacing a gas furnace with an electric heat pump is now the highest-ROI energy move available. The math, the climate considerations, and the federal stacking opportunities.

UB

**Reviewed by UtilityBenefits Editorial Team** Energy & utilities research desk · cited primary sources

**Last reviewed** May 4, 2026

Quick Answer · Speakable schema

Modern heat pumps operate at **250–400% efficiency** vs. gas furnaces at 80–95%. In moderate climates, heat pumps cut total heating costs by **30–50%** even after accounting for higher electricity prices. In cold climates (below 0°F regularly), modern cold-climate heat pumps still work but a **hybrid system** (heat pump + small gas backup) is often the right answer. Federal IRA stacking covers **$14,000+** of installation costs for income-qualified households via 25C tax credit + HEEHRA rebate + state energy office rebates + utility rebates. For most households this is now the single biggest energy-savings move available.

How heat pumps work (the brief version)
---------------------------------------

A heat pump is just a reversible air conditioner. In summer, it pulls heat out of your house. In winter, it pulls heat _into_ your house from the outside air. The "outside air is cold" objection is a misunderstanding — even -10°F air contains plenty of heat energy from a thermodynamic standpoint, and modern heat pumps efficiently extract it.

The efficiency math:

*   Resistance heater (electric baseboard, electric furnace): **100% efficient**. 1 kWh in, 1 kWh of heat out.
*   Modern gas furnace: **90–98% AFUE**. Roughly 95% of the gas energy becomes useful heat.
*   Modern heat pump: **250–400% COP**. 1 kWh in, 2.5–4 kWh of heat out (because most of the energy comes from the outside air, not the electricity).
*   Modern cold-climate heat pump at -15°F: **200–250% COP** (still beats resistance heating by 2–2.5×).

Operating cost math
-------------------

The real question is total annual heating cost. This depends on climate (heating degree days), local energy prices, and system efficiency. Rough 2026 numbers for a 2,000 sq ft home with 70 million BTU/year of heating demand:

| System | Climate zone | Annual heating cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 80% AFUE gas furnace (old) | Boston-area (5,500 HDD) | $1,800 – $2,400 |
| 95% AFUE gas furnace (new) | Boston-area | $1,500 – $2,000 |
| Standard heat pump | Boston-area | $1,300 – $1,800 |
| Cold-climate heat pump | Boston-area | $1,100 – $1,500 |
| Hybrid (HP + gas backup) | Boston-area | $1,200 – $1,600 |
| 80% AFUE gas furnace | Atlanta-area (2,500 HDD) | $700 – $1,000 |
| Standard heat pump | Atlanta-area | $400 – $700 |
| 80% AFUE gas furnace | Minneapolis-area (8,000 HDD) | $2,500 – $3,500 |
| Cold-climate heat pump | Minneapolis-area | $1,800 – $2,500 |
| Hybrid system | Minneapolis-area | $1,800 – $2,400 |

Indicative ranges based on 2026 fuel prices ($1.20/therm gas, 14¢/kWh electric). Actual costs depend on home insulation, thermostat behavior, equipment sizing, and local utility rates.

The pattern: **heat pumps win in moderate climates by a wide margin** (Atlanta, Charlotte, Dallas, most of CA). **Heat pumps win modestly in cold climates** (Boston, Chicago, Detroit) — by maybe $200–$400/year. **Hybrid systems win in extreme cold** (Minneapolis, Burlington VT, Fargo) — heat pump runs most of the year, small gas backup handles the polar-vortex weeks.

Federal IRA stacking math
-------------------------

The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act created the most generous heat pump incentive program in U.S. history. The available stack:

| Program | Heat pump benefit | Eligibility |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Federal 25C tax credit | $2,000/year | Any taxpayer with income tax owed |
| HEEHRA rebate (heat pump) | $8,000 | ≤80% Area Median Income (AMI) |
| HEEHRA rebate (electrical panel) | $4,000 | If panel upgrade needed for HP install |
| State energy office rebates | $1,000 – $4,000 | Varies by state, mostly launching 2025–2026 |
| Utility rebates | $500 – $3,000 | Most utilities have at least basic HP rebates |
| HOMES Rebate (whole-home) | $8,000 | For deep retrofits, low-income |

For an income-qualified household installing a $16,000 cold-climate heat pump system:

*   HEEHRA rebate: $8,000
*   State energy office: $2,000
*   Utility rebate: $1,500
*   Federal 25C tax credit: $2,000
*   **Net cost: $2,500 (84% covered)**

For a non-income-qualified household installing the same system:

*   State energy office: $2,000
*   Utility rebate: $1,500
*   Federal 25C tax credit: $2,000
*   **Net cost: $10,500 (34% covered)**

HEEHRA and state programs roll out at different paces. CA, NY, MA, CO, MN, GA, ME launched first. Most others launching through late 2025 and into 2026. Check your state energy office website for current availability.

When a gas furnace still makes sense
------------------------------------

*   **Your existing furnace is recent (under 10 years old) and working well.** Replacing a young furnace doesn't make economic sense. Wait until end of life, then evaluate heat pump vs new furnace.
*   **You live in extreme cold (regularly below -15°F) and don't want a hybrid system.** Even modern cold-climate heat pumps lose efficiency at extreme cold; a hybrid is usually better but adds complexity.
*   **Your electric service is undersized.** Many older homes have 100A panels. A heat pump conversion may require a $2,000–$4,000 panel upgrade. HEEHRA covers this for income-qualified households; otherwise it's an additional cost.
*   **You're moving in <5 years.** Payback periods are 5–12 years depending on stacking. If you won't be there to recoup, the math weakens.
*   **You have free fuel.** Some farms and rural homes have free or very-cheap natural gas, propane, or wood. Heat pumps still beat resistance heat but lose to free fuel.

When a heat pump is the obvious answer
--------------------------------------

*   **Your existing furnace is 15+ years old.** End of life is replacement time anyway — heat pump is now the obvious choice in most climates.
*   **You live in a moderate climate.** Most of CA, the Southeast (excluding TX deep south), the mid-Atlantic, the Pacific Northwest — heat pumps dominate the operating cost math.
*   **You have an existing AC unit that's also old.** A heat pump replaces both AC and furnace with one system. Combined replacement is cheaper than separate units.
*   **You're income-qualified for HEEHRA.** 84% covered makes the math compelling regardless of climate.
*   **You care about climate impact.** Heat pumps have ~50% lower emissions than gas heating in most U.S. grids, declining further as the grid decarbonizes.

Cold-climate heat pump models worth knowing
-------------------------------------------

Not all heat pumps perform the same in cold weather. The leaders for cold-climate performance (rated for -15°F or colder):

*   **Mitsubishi Hyper-Heat / H2i** — long track record, available in ducted and ductless; widely installed in MA, ME, MN.
*   **LG XCool / Multi V** — strong cold-climate performance; aggressive pricing.
*   **Carrier Greenspeed Infinity** — wider U.S. distribution; ducted-focus.
*   **Bosch IDS** — mid-priced with good cold-climate ratings.
*   **Trane XV / XL Series** — wide distribution; somewhat behind Mitsubishi/LG on extreme cold.

Talk to a local installer about which models they support — installer experience matters more than spec-sheet differences. NEEP (Northeast Energy Efficiency Partnerships) maintains a public list of cold-climate heat pump models.

FAQ
---

Can a heat pump really keep up in below-zero weather?

Modern cold-climate heat pumps (NEEP-listed models) operate efficiently down to -15°F to -20°F. Below that, efficiency drops but they still work. For climates with regular extended periods below -15°F, a hybrid system (heat pump + small gas furnace backup) is the typical solution. Maine, Vermont, and Minnesota all have growing heat-pump installation bases — they work in cold weather.

Will my electric bill go up if I switch to a heat pump?

Yes, your electric bill goes up — but your gas bill goes to near-zero (just water heating and cooking, if those are still gas). Total energy bill typically drops 30–50% in moderate climates, 10–25% in cold climates. Run the numbers for your specific situation before deciding.

What about water heating?

Heat pump water heaters exist and are now mainstream — 250–300% efficiency vs. gas water heaters at 60–80%. HEEHRA covers up to $1,750 for HP water heaters; federal 25C covers $600. Stack with utility rebates. If you're converting heating, do the water heater at the same time.

How long does heat pump installation take?

Typical retrofit: 2–4 days of work, plus possibly an electrical panel upgrade (1 day). Permits and contractor scheduling can stretch the calendar to 4–8 weeks from quote to completion.

What's a hybrid system?

A heat pump paired with a smaller gas furnace as backup. Heat pump handles 80–95% of the heating year (above ~20°F outdoor temp); gas furnace kicks in only during extreme cold. Captures most of the heat pump efficiency advantage while keeping gas as a safety net for polar-vortex weeks. Common in cold-climate retrofits.

Can renters do this?

Generally no — heat pump installation requires homeowner authorization. Renters can ask landlords, especially when an existing furnace fails. Some states have landlord-targeted incentive programs to encourage HP installations in rental properties.

What if I'm in an apartment?

Mini-split (ductless) heat pumps are the typical apartment solution. One outdoor unit feeds 1–4 indoor units, no ductwork needed. Easier to install in older buildings. Owners and condo boards can install; renters need landlord cooperation.

Standard air-source heat pumps lose efficiency below 40°F and struggle below 25°F, according to one 2026 cost guide.

claims.claim: Cold-climate heat pumps maintain efficiency down to 5°F and continue operating at -15°F, though at reduced capacity, according to one 2026 cost guide.

claims.claim: There is no official 'cold climate' standard for heat pumps, according to Consumer Reports.
Energy Star has a cold-climate certification mark for air-source heat pumps signifying suitable low-temperature performance and efficiency.
claims.scope: Energy Star air-source heat pump program

claims.claim: Under Energy Star, cold-climate heat pumps must demonstrate low ambient performance and meet specified HSPF2 and SEER2 thresholds; for ducted split systems the thresholds are at least 8.1 HSPF2 and 15.2 SEER2.
claims.scope: Energy Star air-source heat pump criteria

claims.claim: NEEP maintains a Cold Climate Air Source Heat Pump (ccASHP) product list and specifications to provide standardized cold-climate performance data.
In very cold climates, a dual-fuel system pairs a cold-climate heat pump with a gas furnace backup.
A dual-fuel thermostat typically switches from the heat pump to the furnace at a changeover temperature of 25–35°F.
In a dual-fuel setup, the heat pump handles most heating needs and switches to the furnace during very cold weather.
A dual-fuel system can have the heat pump handle 80–95% of the heating year above about 20°F outdoor temperature, with the gas furnace used only during extreme cold.

A dual-fuel system is not automatically cheaper; its economics depend on gas price, electric rate, heat pump efficiency, furnace efficiency, and switch temperature, and a wrong lockout setting can erase savings.

Dual-fuel operation shuts off the heat pump when the gas furnace activates with no parallel operation, while a cold-climate heat pump with electric strip heat continues running at reduced capacity and strips cover only the gap below the balance point.
claims.option: dual-fuel vs ccASHP plus electric strip

claims.claim: Even in milder parts of the U.S. where temperatures only occasionally drop below freezing, basic single-speed heat pumps are often paired with a backup heating system; in cold climates a backup or hybrid system may be needed.

For national average rates ($0.14/kWh electricity, $1.20/therm gas, 92% AFUE furnace), the break-even COP is approximately 2.1, corresponding to about 25–30°F for standard heat pumps and 15–20°F for cold-climate heat pumps; above that temperature the heat pump is cheaper, below it the gas furnace is cheaper.
claims.scope: national average rates, 2026, per HVAC Calculator Hub

claims.claim: In a Zone 4 climate at national average energy prices, a high-efficiency cold-climate heat pump (HSPF2 11.0) costs about $620/year for heating versus about $720/year for a 96 AFUE gas furnace, roughly $100/year less.
claims.option: cold-climate heat pump vs gas furnace
claims.scope: Zone 4, national average energy prices, example

claims.claim: In very cold climates with higher electricity rates, a heat pump may not save on heating versus a modern high-efficiency gas furnace, though it may still save on cooling and eliminate natural gas infrastructure costs.
claims.scope: very cold climates with higher electricity rates

claims.claim: In mild to moderate climates, a heat pump is often cheaper to run; in areas with high electricity rates or extreme cold, a natural gas furnace may be more economical.
claims.criterion: operating cost by climate and electricity rate

claims.claim: Chicago is about as far north as PickHVAC recommends using a heat pump versus a gas furnace; colder climates make heat pumps less efficient and more likely to use backup/auxiliary heating strips that drive up operating costs.
Upfront installed costs are approximately $4,000–$8,000 for a standard heat pump, $6,000–$12,000 for a cold-climate model, and $3,000–$7,000 for a gas furnace.
Heat pumps provide both heating and cooling, potentially eliminating a separate $3,000–$5,000 AC unit.

In a Minneapolis case study (2,200 sq ft, 7,500 heating degree days), gas furnace replacement was $5,500, a cold-climate heat pump was $11,200, a HEEHRA rebate was -$4,000, and net additional cost for the heat pump was $1,700.
claims.option: cold-climate heat pump vs gas furnace

claims.claim: Federal Section 25C tax credits and utility rebates can offset $1,500–$4,000 of the heat pump's equipment premium.

In a Massachusetts example, a 3-ton cold-climate ASHP installed for $10,000 with a $3,000 Mass Save rebate and a $2,000 federal 25C credit (30%, capped at $2,000) has a net out-of-pocket cost of $5,000.
New utility rebates favor hybrid systems that combine cold-climate heat pumps with gas furnaces for better efficiency in cold weather.

An HVAC rebate guide recommends that if a home has a heating load over 40,000 BTU/hr and is in a cold climate (below 5°F design temperature), the homeowner should pair a heat pump with a gas furnace (dual-fuel) to maximize rebates and comfort.
claims.scope: cold climate, over 40,000 BTU/hr, below 5°F design temperature

claims.claim: For most homeowners, a high-efficiency heat pump offers the best rebate value and long-term energy savings, according to an HVAC rebate guide.
The same guide says that in very cold climates a dual-fuel system should be considered.
claims.scope: very cold climates, per HVAC Database

claims.claim: A 96% AFUE gas furnace converts 96 cents of each dollar of gas into usable heat, while an 80% AFUE furnace wastes 20 cents; the difference between 80% and 96% AFUE saves approximately $150–$400 per year on a typical cold-climate gas bill.

In very cold weather, a condensing furnace (90%+ AFUE) can lose some efficiency because cold combustion air chills heat exchanger surfaces and may cause excessive condensation or freezing of the condensate drain; actual seasonal efficiency in extreme climates may be 2–4% lower than rated AFUE.
All furnaces in one 2026 comparison meet the minimum 96% AFUE efficiency rating recommended for cold climates.
Modulating furnaces provide the best comfort and efficiency for extreme cold climates by adjusting output in small increments, according to a furnace buying guide.
claims.scope: extreme cold climates, per that guide

recommendations.choose: Choose a dual-fuel system that pairs a cold-climate heat pump with a gas furnace backup.
recommendations.when: When your home is in a very cold climate with a design temperature below 5°F or a heating load over 40,000 BTU/hr, and you want to maximize rebates and comfort while retaining a gas backup for extreme cold.

recommendations.choose: Choose a cold-climate heat pump as the primary heating system, with backup only as required by a Manual J load calculation.
recommendations.when: When the climate is cold but not extreme, electricity rates are favorable, applicable rebates are available, and you also value the cooling the heat pump provides.

recommendations.choose: Choose a high-efficiency gas furnace, preferably 96% AFUE or higher and possibly modulating.
recommendations.when: When natural gas is cheap, electricity rates are high, the climate is severe, or you want the lowest upfront cost and a simple system, especially if you plan to move within a few years.
